title: Bail Confirmed on 45 days delay in Lodging FIR
explainer:
This case involves Muhammad Rafique, who was accused of stealing four cattle from a complainant's shed in Multan. An FIR was registered against him and another person under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with theft and dishonestly receiving stolen property. However, the FIR was filed one and a half months after the cattle went missing, and this delay was never explained by the complainant.

The Lahore High Court found several problems with the prosecution's case. There was no explanation of how the complainant suddenly came to know that the petitioner was involved in the theft. Additionally, the investigating officer admitted that the stolen cattle had actually been recovered earlier under a separate legal provision, having been left behind by unidentified persons, well before the FIR was even filed. This raised doubts about whether the story linking the petitioner to the crime was genuine.

The court also noted that the investigating officer confirmed nothing remained to be recovered from the petitioner, that the investigation was already complete, and that the case had been sent to trial but had not yet begun. The petitioner had no prior criminal record, and the charges did not fall under the more serious category of offenses that would normally block bail.

Given these doubts and the lack of prior convictions, the court ruled that the matter required further inquiry at trial and confirmed the petitioner's pre-arrest bail, requiring him to post a bond of Rs. 50,000 with a surety.

title: Jurisdiction of High Court in cases of Promotion of Civil Servants
explainer:
This case concerns a civil servant, Nawabzada Muhammad Nadir Khan Hoti, who was passed over for promotion to a senior grade (BPS-21) by the Central Selection Board (CSB). The Board's reasons included allegations that he was involved in improper sales tax refunds and did not enjoy a good reputation. However, the petitioner showed that these very allegations had earlier been withdrawn by the tax department itself, and an inquiry against him had been vacated, meaning no charges were actually pending against him when the CSB made its decision.

The government argued that the Peshawar High Court had no jurisdiction to hear the case, since civil servants' service matters are normally handled by the Federal Service Tribunal, and since the decision was made in Islamabad, not within the court's territorial area. The court rejected both objections. It held that questions about a civil servant's "fitness" for promotion are excluded from the Service Tribunal's jurisdiction and can be examined by the High Court, and that territorial jurisdiction under Article 199 is not limited by ordinary civil procedure rules when federal bodies operate nationwide.

On the merits, the court found that the CSB acted unfairly by relying on discredited allegations without giving the petitioner evidence or a chance to respond, violating the fundamental right to fair and transparent procedure under Article 10-A. The court ruled in his favor, following a similar precedent from the same CSB meeting, reinforcing that promotion decisions must be based on solid, verified evidence and fair procedure.

title: Competency of Revenue Courts in case of Eviction of Tenant
explainer:
This case is from the Supreme Court of Pakistan and deals with a dispute between a landlord and his agricultural tenant over unpaid rent and eviction.

The landlord sued the tenant to recover unpaid rent for several years and to evict him from the leased agricultural land, on the grounds that the tenant had defaulted on rent payments. The Assistant Collector ruled against the tenant, ordering him to pay a large sum in arrears and vacate the land. The tenant then appealed and sought review at multiple levels, including the Collector, the Commissioner, the Board of Revenue, and the Peshawar High Court, but lost at every stage. He then asked the Supreme Court for permission to appeal.

The tenant raised several arguments: that the Revenue Court had no authority to hear the case at all; that he was not actually a defaulter; that the landlord had never handed over the full area of land promised, so his rent should be reduced proportionately; and that he deserved compensation for buildings he had constructed on the land.

The Supreme Court rejected all these arguments. It confirmed that Revenue Courts were indeed the proper forum for such tenancy disputes under the relevant tenancy law. It agreed with the lower courts' factual findings that the tenant was in default, that there had been no short delivery of land, and that since the tenant built structures without the landlord's consent, he was not entitled to compensation for them.

title: Powers of Court in Execution Proceedings
explainer:
This case dealt with how far courts can go to enforce a maintenance decree issued by a Family Court, and whether people connected to the actual debtor, like his attorney or a surety, could escape responsibility for the unpaid amount.

A Family Court had ordered Qamar-uz-Zaman to pay maintenance to his minor child. His brother, Farooq Ahmed, acted as his attorney and handled the case throughout. When Farooq failed to pay the full decretal amount, he was sent to civil prison but released after paying part of it and providing a surety (Mehboob Ahmed) for the rest. Later, Qamar-uz-Zaman returned from abroad, cancelled the power of attorney, and claimed he was not responsible. Both the attorney and the surety also tried to get released from liability, but the Executing Court and the Additional District Judge rejected their applications, holding them responsible for the balance. They then challenged this in the Lahore High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, ruling that the attorney and surety's liability is coextensive with that of the judgment debtor, since the attorney had actively pursued the case and the surety had voluntarily accepted responsibility. It held that decrees, especially from Family Courts, must be enforced effectively, using recovery procedures similar to those for land revenue arrears, and that debtors cannot use technicalities to escape execution.

title: Penalty in Rent Agreement is Prohibited under Section 11 of IRRO

explainer:

The landlord had filed for the tenant's eviction, alleging default in rent payments, violation of the lease agreement, and personal need for the property. Both the Rent Controller and the Additional District Judge ruled in favor of the landlord, ordering the tenant to vacate.

The tenant challenged this before the Islamabad High Court, arguing that he had made repeated genuine efforts to pay rent through money orders and courier services, but the landlord had refused to accept them. The eviction order was largely based on the tenant's failure to pay a contractual fine of Rs. 500 per day for late rent payment, and on his failure to pay a rent increase that the landlord claimed had automatically taken effect.

The High Court found that the Rs. 500 daily charge was actually a penalty, not rent, and that Section 11 of the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001 specifically prohibits such penalty clauses in rent agreements, making that part of the agreement void from the start. The court also noted the landlord had never issued a proper notice demanding the increased statutory rent or applied to strike off the tenant's defence, so that ground could not be used either.

title: Latest Judgment in a Defamation Case
citation: PLD 1981 Kar. 515; Mazhar Valjee v. Sher Afghan Khan Niazi 2004 YLR
explainer:
This case involved a defamation lawsuit brought by the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan against a newspaper, Khabrain, and its publishers (Liberty Papers Ltd). The newspaper had published a story on 8 March 2004 falsely and maliciously claiming that office bearers of the Human Rights Commission were instigating violence, spreading anti-military sentiments through financial rewards, and that certain groups were subsidiaries of the organization. The trial court awarded the Commission five million rupees in damages, and on appeal the Balochistan High Court reduced this to one million rupees. The newspaper then appealed to the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, dismissing the newspaper's appeal. It held that the allegations were serious because they accused public figures of conspiring against the state through underhanded means, and that the newspaper had nationwide circulation, causing significant reputational and financial harm. The Court also clarified important legal principles: plaintiffs in defamation cases can sue wherever the material was published or significantly circulated; newspapers must prove they acted diligently and followed ethical journalistic standards to claim a "good faith" defense; and failure to prove the truth of published claims can itself indicate malice, justifying aggravated damages. The judgment emphasizes that protecting personal dignity is a constitutional obligation, and media freedom does not excuse irresponsible or unverified reporting.

title: Zina Case Judgment
explainer:
This case is about a man, Muhammad Ashiq, who tried to bring a criminal complaint of qazf (false accusation of zina, meaning unlawful sexual intercourse) against Haji Abdul Razzaq, Mst. Kalsoom Mai, and others under Pakistan's Offence of Qazf Ordinance, 1979.

The background: Kalsoom Mai had earlier filed a petition alleging that Ashiq and others committed zina-bil-jabr against her. Police investigated and found her allegations false, and she later withdrew the petition, with reports suggesting the parties had reached a compromise. Ashiq then filed his own complaint accusing her and others of qazf, arguing they had falsely accused him. A trial court judge dismissed his complaint at the outset, noting he waited 21 months to file it and that legal requirements for a qazf case were not met.

On appeal, the Federal Shariat Court upheld the dismissal. It found that Kalsoom Mai never appeared in court or gave any statement, so there was no formal finding by any court that she had lied or made a false accusation, which is required under the law. The mere fact her original complaint included her photograph did not prove she authored it. The court also noted Ashiq and his co-accused had been acquitted in the related criminal case due to doubts in the prosecution's evidence, not because anyone was proven to have lied.

title: Quashing of FIR Judgment
explainer:
This case is about a petition asking the Sindh High Court to cancel a First Information Report (FIR) registered against Wajid Ali Memon and others under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with rioting, criminal force, wrongful restraint, criminal intimidation, and also under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The FIR arose from an incident where a Magistrate, acting on court orders to search for a missing person, was blocked by a crowd at a house, faced threats, and had someone attempt to snatch his guard's weapon. Based on this report, a Single Judge had earlier directed police to register an FIR, including charges under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The Division Bench of the High Court, hearing the petition to quash the FIR, examined the facts and found that the elements required for terrorism charges (Sections 6/7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act) and for criminal intimidation (Section 506(ii) PPC) were not actually present, since mere threats without the specific ingredients of criminal intimidation are not enough. The court ruled these particular sections should be deleted from the case, meaning it would be handled by a regular court instead of an anti-terrorism court.

However, the court did not quash the entire FIR. It held that quashing an FIR is only appropriate when the evidence, even if fully believed, could not support any conviction. Since the case was still pending trial, the petitioner was told to pursue his remedies before the trial court instead.

title: Perjury is not allowed in the court of law
explainer:
This Supreme Court of Pakistan judgment dealt with the case of Muhammad Aslam, who was convicted of murdering his uncle, Mehdi Hassan. The motive was revenge: years earlier, when Aslam was a small child, his father had disappeared and was suspected to have been killed by his own step-brother, the same Mehdi Hassan. When Aslam grew into his teens, he shot and killed Mehdi Hassan in public, declaring he had avenged his father's death.

The Lahore High Court had upheld his conviction and death sentence. The Supreme Court agreed he was guilty but reduced his sentence from death to life imprisonment, taking into account that he committed the act while still very young, avenging a killing that had happened when he was only two or three years old. However, the Court found the fine imposed too low and raised it from Rs. 2,000 to Rs. 25,000, to be paid as compensation to the deceased's heirs if recovered.

Separately, the Court addressed perjury. It found that two witnesses, one for the prosecution and one for the defence, had lied under oath during the trial. The judges strongly condemned false testimony, stressing that courts must punish perjury firmly to deter others, since lying in court undermines public trust in the justice system. The Supreme Court directed the trial court to initiate proceedings against both witnesses under the law dealing with false evidence.

title: Justice of Peace is not required to allow petition blindly
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a dispute over the registration of a criminal case (FIR) by police. The petitioner, Qamar Naeem, claimed he owned a shop that he had rented out to another person. He alleged that certain accused individuals, armed with weapons, forcibly broke the lock of the shop and attacked him. When he approached the police to register a case, they instead began an inquiry rather than registering an FIR. He then approached the Justice of Peace under Section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking for a direction to register the case, but this request was rejected.

The High Court found that the facts described by the petitioner clearly disclosed a cognizable offence, meaning the police had a legal duty to register an FIR without first investigating or hearing the accused's side. The court explained that while a Justice of Peace has power to review such police inaction, this power is limited: he should not dive into disputed facts, nor should he approve or reject requests automatically without proper legal reasoning. However, if the complainant's allegations clearly show a cognizable offence, refusing to register the case is arbitrary and improper.

The court therefore quashed the Justice of Peace's order and directed the police to register the FIR. This judgment matters because it clarifies the limited role of a Justice of Peace and reinforces those with genuine complaints disclosing criminal offences cannot be denied FIR registration through overly cautious or dismissive judicial review.

title: Custody of Minor by Grandmother
explainer:
This case was about who should have custody of a young boy after his father died: his mother or his paternal grandmother. After the father's death, the mother lived with her in-laws, but the grandmother later forced her out of the house while keeping the child. The mother first sought the child's recovery through the courts, but her petition was dismissed because the boy said he preferred living with his grandmother. She then filed a separate case asking to be made his legal guardian, which was also initially dismissed on the same grounds. On appeal, though, the earlier decision was overturned, and the court ordered that custody be given to the mother. The grandmother challenged this in the High Court.

The High Court upheld the decision in the mother's favor. It found that the child appeared to have been influenced against his mother, even inventing false claims of abuse, and that the grandmother had not followed the court's visitation arrangements and seemed to be encouraging the child to lie and harbor hatred. The judge stressed that harm to a child isn't only physical but can be psychological too. It noted the mother's sacrifices, her stability, and that under Islamic law a grandmother's right to custody is secondary to the mother's. Ultimately, the court held that the child's true welfare lay with his mother, and dismissed the grandmother's petition. The case underscores that in custody disputes, the child's actual best interests—not just their stated preference—must guide the court's decision.

title: Judgment on Inheritance of Consanguine Sisters
explainer:
This case involves a dispute over inheritance following the death of Ali Haider Khan, who died without children. His widow and one full sister (the appellants) claimed they alone were entitled to his property, arguing that his other siblings, described as step-brothers and step-sisters, should be excluded as residuary heirs under Islamic inheritance law. The respondents were these step-siblings, who had also applied for a succession certificate to claim their share.

The trial court had already divided the estate: the widow received one-fourth, the full sister received one-half, and the remaining share was split among the four step-brothers and two step-sisters. The widow and sister appealed, arguing that under Mohammadan Law, specifically Section 109, uterine (half) siblings sharing only a mother with the deceased are excluded from inheriting any "return" share if a full sister exists.

The High Court dismissed the appeal. It clarified that Section 109 only excludes uterine siblings, not consanguine siblings, who share a father with the deceased. Since the respondents were consanguine, not uterine, siblings, the rule the appellants relied on did not apply to them. The court also noted that a party cannot argue a position contrary to what it originally pleaded.

This judgment matters because it clarifies an important distinction in Islamic inheritance law between uterine and consanguine siblings, confirming that consanguine siblings are not automatically excluded from inheritance shares even when a full sister survives the deceased.

title: Direct Appeal against Election Petition Allowed by Supreme Court
explainer:
This case is about a challenge to the 2008 National Assembly election result from a constituency in Khushab, Punjab. Malik Umar Aslam, who lost narrowly to Mrs. Sumaira Malik, filed an election petition alleging vote manipulation and, crucially, that Malik's BA degree - required at the time to qualify as a candidate - was fake, obtained through impersonation rather than her actually sitting the exams.

The Election Tribunal had dismissed his petition, so he appealed directly to the Supreme Court under the Representation of the People Act, 1976.

The Supreme Court examined evidence including signatures, photographs on university admission and registration forms, and attendance records, comparing them under the Qanun-e-Shahadat (evidence law). It found that the degree had indeed been secured through impersonation and fraud, meaning Malik did not actually meet the graduation requirement in place for the 2002 elections under the Conduct of General Election Order. The Court held that a candidate must satisfy the constitutional character requirements of being honest, righteous and non-profligate, and that obtaining a degree through fraud meant she failed this test and was never validly qualified to hold the seat.

As a result, the Court ruled she was not lawfully holding her seat, could not benefit from the disputed election, and would be barred from contesting future elections too - with the Election Commission required to unseat her if she were ever declared elected again. This case is significant because it reinforced strict scrutiny of candidates' educational credentials and moral qualifications for public office.

title: Concept of Suspension of Sentence
explainer:
This Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) decision deals with a technical but important procedural question: when can a High Court suspend a criminal sentence and release a convicted person on bail while their case is pending before the Supreme Court?

The relevant law is Section 426(2B) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows a High Court to suspend a sentence and grant bail if a convicted person has been granted "special leave to appeal" against a sentence the High Court itself imposed or upheld. A Deputy Prosecutor General had objected to this provision being used, apparently confusing "special leave to appeal" with a "certificate" that a High Court can issue confirming a case is fit for appeal to the Supreme Court.

The court clarified that these are two entirely different things. "Special leave to appeal" (now called "leave to appeal") can only be granted by the Supreme Court itself, under its constitutional and procedural powers—no High Court has authority to grant it. A High Court can only certify that a case involves a substantial legal question, which is a separate mechanism under Article 185 of the Constitution. The court traced the history of these provisions through the Constitution and Supreme Court Rules to support its reasoning.

Having clarified this distinction, the court overruled the prosecutor's objection, confirming that once the Supreme Court grants leave to appeal, the High Court retains power under Section 426(2B) to suspend the sentence and grant bail pending that appeal. This clarifies procedural rights for convicts awaiting Supreme Court appeals.

title: The base of Khula is verse 229 of Surah Al Baqrah
explainer:
This case is from the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court, deciding an appeal about a divorce dispute between a husband and wife. The wife had filed for dissolution of her marriage on grounds of cruelty, mental torture, non-payment of maintenance, and khula (a wife's Islamic right to seek separation from her husband). The husband opposed this and filed his own suit demanding restitution of conjugal rights, insisting his wife return to him. He also claimed that if khula were granted, his wife should return gold jewelry, household items, and dower money he had given her.

The trial court (Family Court, Mirpur) had already ruled in the wife's favor, granting the divorce through khula and dismissing the husband's case for restitution of conjugal rights. The husband appealed this decision to the High Court.

The High Court explained the Islamic legal basis for khula, tracing it to verse 229 of Surah Al-Baqarah in the Quran. It held that before granting khula, a court must be satisfied that the spouses cannot realistically continue their marriage happily within the moral and religious limits set by Islamic teaching, that the wife genuinely wants separation, and that she is willing to return consideration (such as dower) as required. Whether reconciliation is possible is a factual question depending on each case's circumstances.

This judgment is significant because it clarifies the religious and legal reasoning courts must apply when deciding khula cases, emphasizing that such decisions require careful factual assessment rather than automatic grants or refusals.

title: Khula is Islamic Right of a wife
explainer:
This case involved a husband challenging a court decision that granted his wife a divorce through khula, an Islamic legal mechanism allowing a wife to end her marriage. The wife had earlier filed a similar suit that was withdrawn after the couple reconciled and agreed to live together again, but the marriage broke down once more due to alleged mistreatment, so she filed a fresh suit. The trial court dissolved the marriage on condition she return the dower she had received.

The husband argued the second suit should not have been allowed since the first was withdrawn due to compromise, and also argued that the law allowing courts to grant khula without full evidence violated Islamic principles and his right to a fair trial.

The Lahore High Court rejected both arguments. It held that rules under the Civil Procedure Code barring repeat suits after withdrawal do not apply to family court cases, and that the wife's claims of renewed cruelty and hatred created a new cause of action, making her second suit valid. The court also held that khula is rooted in Quranic teaching, and that forcing spouses to remain in a hateful marriage causes social harm. If a wife firmly states she cannot maintain the marriage within God's limits, courts may accept this and dissolve the marriage. The petition was dismissed, upholding the wife's divorce and affirming khula as a legitimate Islamic right exercised through the family courts.

The FIR alleged that armed men hijacked an oil tanker carrying diesel worth lakhs of rupees, assaulting the driver and conductor before driving off with the vehicle and its cargo. The petitioners were later implicated under Sections 395 (dacoity) and 412 (receiving stolen property in a dacoity) of the Pakistan Penal Code, though they were not named in the original FIR and were only linked to the crime through a co-accused's statement during investigation.

The Islamabad High Court examined the legal definitions of dacoity, robbery, and theft, noting that dacoity requires proof that five or more people acted together in committing the offence. The court found that the prosecution had not gathered sufficient evidence connecting these petitioners specifically to the dacoity charge, and the claim about proceeds from selling the stolen diesel remained unproven and unclear. The court also noted that certain admissions relied upon by police were not legally admissible as evidence under the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order.

Importantly, the court pointed out that co-accused with similar roles in the same case had already been granted bail by the same court. Applying the principle of consistency, meaning similar cases should be treated alike, the court granted bail to these two petitioners as well. title: Tariq Aziz promotion case on Employment Law
explainer:
This case was decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan and involved civil servants in Basic Scale-21 who challenged the promotions of certain colleagues to Basic Scale-22, arguing the process was unfair and arbitrary.

The petitioners pointed out that under Rule 15(2) of the Rules of Business, 1973, any case for the Prime Minister's decision on such promotions was required to be submitted through a self-contained, concise and objective summary covering the relevant facts. However, it emerged that for roughly 60 years, this rule had simply not been followed. Instead, files were sent to the Prime Minister without proper summaries, and only the files of some officers were forwarded, while others equally or more deserving were left out without any recorded justification.

The Supreme Court held that this practice violated the law and denied fairness and transparency to officers who were sidelined without their merit being considered. While civil servants have no absolute right to promotion, the Court held they do have a genuine right, under the Civil Servants Act, 1973, to have their case properly considered based on merit and service record.

The Court set aside the promotion notifications, declared them legally ineffective, and directed the government to reconsider all eligible officers afresh, fairly and transparently. It also recommended reviving proper rules for such decisions. This case matters because it reinforces that government promotions must follow due process and cannot be based on arbitrary or selective treatment.

title: Unfair Labor Practice Petition against PIA
explainer:
This case involved airline employees of Pakistan International Airlines Corporation (PIA) who filed petitions before the National Industrial Relations Commission (NIRC) in Islamabad after being transferred from one office to another, including a transfer from Islamabad to Karachi. The employees argued that these transfers amounted to unfair labour practice and asked the Commission to stop PIA from taking such action against them or to reverse any such orders already made.

The Commission examined the relevant law, particularly Section 31 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 2011, which lists specific actions considered unfair labour practices by employers, mainly relating to interference with trade union rights and membership. The Commission also looked at PIA's own service regulations, which explicitly allow the corporation to transfer employees within or outside Pakistan as needed for its operations.

The Commission ruled that transferring employees is a normal management right, allowing the employer to decide how best to use its staff in the company's and public interest. This right cannot be overridden unless there is solid, convincing evidence that the transfer was done to victimize an employee or was genuinely connected to unfair labour practice, such as anti-union discrimination. Vague or general complaints are not enough to prove this.

Since the employees did not provide such specific evidence, the Commission found no unfair labour practice had occurred and dismissed their petitions. This case is significant because it clarifies that routine administrative transfers by employers are lawful unless proven to be retaliatory or discriminatory under labour law.

title: Limitation is three years to demand dowry articles (Article 49)
explainer:
This case involved a wife suing her ex-husband to recover her dowry articles, or their cash equivalent, after their marriage ended in divorce. The couple married in 1987, and the husband divorced her in 1989. In 1992, she filed a suit claiming the husband had kept her dowry items and refused to return them despite her demands, valuing them at Rs. 24,800. The trial court and the appellate court both ruled in her favor, and the husband challenged this in the Lahore High Court.

The husband argued the suit was filed too late, that delivery of the dowry items to him was never proven, and that the amount awarded was too high. The High Court rejected all three arguments. On the facts, it held that the lower courts had properly weighed the evidence, including testimony from the wife and three witnesses, while the husband's sister, defending the case on his behalf, failed to meaningfully rebut this evidence. Such factual findings, the court said, are not something a revision court should reopen.

On the legal question, the court clarified how limitation works for dowry recovery suits under Article 49 of the Limitation Act. The three-year time limit does not start when the marriage breaks down or the wife leaves the husband's house, but only once the husband's possession becomes "unlawful" - which happens after divorce, and specifically from when the wife demands the items back and the husband refuses. Since the suit was filed within three years of that refusal, it was not time-barred. This ruling matters because it protects women's ability to reclaim dowry property without being unfairly blocked by limitation technicalities.

title: International Lawyer Law Firm
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over a jointly owned house measuring roughly 8 marlas that could not be physically divided among its owners. A partition suit had been filed, and after a preliminary decree was passed by consent of all parties, a court-appointed commissioner reported that the property could not be practically split. One of the co-owners, who had bought and occupied a specific portion of the house, asked for time to purchase the entire property to keep it from being sold to outsiders. She was given multiple opportunities to do so, but eventually her representative admitted she lacked the funds to buy the whole property. The trial court then ordered the property be sold through public auction, and this was upheld on appeal.

She challenged that decision in the Lahore High Court, arguing that auctioning the property before a final decree was improper, and that her specific portion should be separated out since it was more valuable and she would suffer loss if it were sold along with the rest.

The High Court dismissed her petition, holding that once a court finds a property indivisible, the law allows it to be sold and the proceeds distributed among the co-owners, though existing co-owners must first be given the chance to buy out the whole property rather than let it go to an outsider. Since she was given that chance repeatedly and could not raise the funds, the auction order was lawful. The case clarifies how partition and sale of jointly owned indivisible property must proceed under the Partition Act, 1893.

title: Mehboob Alam V. National Radio and Telecom Corporation
explainer:
This case involved two petitioners who challenged how their employment with National Radio and Telecommunication Corporation (NRTC), a government-owned company, was ended.

The first petitioner, a Senior Manager Finance and Company Secretary, had submitted a conditional resignation seeking early retirement with financial benefits after facing friction with a new Managing Director. The Managing Director accepted the resignation immediately, bypassing the proper authority. The petitioner then tried to withdraw his resignation, but this was rejected. Although NRTC's own Board of Directors later set aside the Managing Director's acceptance of the resignation, management ignored the Board's decision and eventually closed the case anyway, without properly involving the petitioner in the inquiry that followed.

The second petitioner, a Chief Engineer, was abruptly retired from service while on approved leave, and his appeal against this was rejected.

NRTC argued the petitions were not maintainable since it was a private limited company, not a government department, and that courts could not intervene under constitutional jurisdiction.

The Peshawar High Court rejected this objection, holding that even employees of such organizations have a right to be heard before adverse action is taken against them, and that bad-faith or malafide actions can be challenged through writ petitions. The court also found that under NRTC's own service rules, only the Board of Directors, not the Managing Director, had authority to accept resignations from employees at the petitioner's grade. The petition was allowed, meaning the petitioner's removal was found unlawful.

title: What is the sanctity of DNA Test - Supreme Court Judgment
explainer:
This case arose from the gang-rape of a 13-year-old girl in Rawalpindi in March 2012. Police initially failed to register an FIR despite the family's complaint, and delays and mishandling by investigators worsened the girl's suffering to the point that she attempted suicide. Media coverage brought the matter to the Supreme Court's attention, which took suo moto notice, ordered an FIR to be registered, and directed an investigation into police misconduct. The case later reached the Court through a constitutional petition raising broader questions about how rape cases are investigated and prosecuted in Pakistan.

The Supreme Court examined the reliability of DNA testing, ruling that while DNA evidence has become a powerful forensic tool, it is not conclusive on its own and must be supported by other evidence. It also held that DNA or medical testing of a victim requires her consent and cannot be forced, as that would violate personal liberty. The Court further ruled that out-of-court settlements in rape cases are invalid, since rape is a non-compoundable offense against society as a whole, not just the individual victim, and the state must pursue prosecution regardless of private settlements.

To improve the justice system's handling of rape cases, the Court issued directions including mandatory preservation of DNA evidence, recording victim statements preferably before female magistrates, holding trials in camera, shielding victims from facing accused persons, and using video conferencing for vulnerable witnesses. This judgment is significant for strengthening protections for rape survivors and improving investigative standards nationwide.

title: What happens when there is delay in FIR?
explainer:
This case involved four men accused of abducting a person, Muhammad Jamil, for ransom and then murdering him. The complainant's brother went missing and was later found dead. The FIR was initially filed against unknown persons, and specific names were added the next day based on information from an unnamed relative who wasn't called to testify in court.

The trial court had acquitted two of the four accused entirely, and while it found insufficient evidence to prove the ransom/abduction charge against the other two, it still convicted them of terrorism and murder, sentencing one (Abdul Ghaffar) to death and another (Sakhawat Ali) to life imprisonment.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court found major weaknesses in the prosecution's case: no one witnessed the crime, the alleged ransom-collection testimony was unconvincing, phone call records that could have identified the culprits were never collected, and a court identification of the accused happened a year late, making it legally unreliable.

However, the court upheld Abdul Ghaffar's murder conviction because the dead body was found buried at his own house after he pointed it out — strong physical evidence connecting him to the killing. The court ruled that murder alone doesn't count as "terrorism" under the Anti-Terrorism Act, so that conviction was dropped. Because the full circumstances remained unclear, his death sentence was reduced to life imprisonment. This case highlights how delays, weak circumstantial evidence, and improper identification procedures can undermine serious criminal charges, even when some evidence still supports guilt.

title: Rights of Individuals are guaranteed in Article 4 of Constitution
explainer:
This case comes from the Federal Shariat Court, dealing with a criminal appeal by two women convicted under the Offence of Zina (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance, 1979. The women had been raided by police at a house allegedly being used as a brothel, based on secret information received by a police inspector.

The court found serious problems with how the police handled the case. The inspector who received the tip did not properly register a First Information Report before acting, then obtained a search warrant through an application the magistrate approved without careful judicial scrutiny, and finally conducted the investigation himself, effectively becoming both complainant and witness. The court held that no law, including the Zina Ordinance or the Criminal Procedure Code, authorizes police to enter a private home merely on suspicion of illicit sex being committed, since this violates the constitutional and Islamic principle of the sanctity of the home and privacy ("chaddar aur chardevari"). The court also noted no independent witnesses from the neighborhood came forward despite the alleged rampant nature of the activity, and no search warrant was actually on record.

Because of these fundamental legal defects, the court held the evidence unreliable and the conviction could not stand. This judgment matters because it reinforces that individual privacy and dignity are protected rights under Article 4 of the Constitution and Islamic injunctions, and that police cannot manufacture cases by violating these protections.

title: Registration of FIR is a right of aggrieved person
explainer:
This case dealt with how police should register a criminal case (FIR) when a citizen complains about wrongdoing by police officials themselves.

A complainant accused two police officers of illegally entering his house, taking money from him during an arrest, and later falsely implicating him in a fraud case after he had cooperated with an FIA inquiry into a separate matter. He approached the Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, who directed the police to register a case against the officers, but specified only certain offences under the Pakistan Penal Code and the Police Order, 2002 which happened to be non-cognizable (meaning police cannot investigate them without court permission).

One of the accused police officers challenged this order, arguing that since the offences named were non-cognizable, the direction to register a case was unlawful.

The Lahore High Court held that it is not for the Justice of Peace to specify particular sections of law while directing registration of a case. Instead, the police have a statutory duty under Section 154 of the Criminal Procedure Code to record any complaint of a cognizable offence and determine themselves what offences are actually disclosed by the facts. The court emphasized that registering an FIR is an independent legal right of any aggrieved person.

The court modified the order, directing the police to record the complainant's statement and register a case if any cognizable offence was found, then investigate accordingly. This ruling reinforces that police cannot avoid registering complaints by narrowly interpreting the offences involved, protecting citizens' access to justice.

title: Police is not possessed with right to murder anyone
explainer:
This case involves a mother's fight to have a murder investigation opened into her son's death at the hands of police. Muhammad Akhtar had married a woman, Mst. Saiqa Bibi, without her family's consent. Her father, a police inspector, was allegedly angered by this and, according to the petitioner, conspired with fellow police officers to kill Akhtar. On 14 March 1997, as Akhtar was heading to Friday prayers, a police head constable allegedly shot and killed him. The police then registered the incident as a "police encounter" (muqabala), officially recording it as a case where Akhtar was killed while resisting arrest, rather than admitting it was a targeted killing.

Akhtar's mother tried repeatedly to get the police to register a murder case against the officers involved, even appealing to the Chief Minister and the press, but no action was taken. She eventually petitioned the Peshawar High Court to order the police to register a First Information Report (FIR) under Section 154 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The court ruled in her favor. It held that police have no right to kill any citizen, regardless of that person's criminal history, and that no one, including police, is above the law. Since the mother's account of a deliberate killing was entirely different from the police's "encounter" version, the court said both versions needed to be investigated separately. It ordered police to register a new FIR based on her complaint, reinforcing that registering an FIR for a cognizable offense is a mandatory legal duty, not a matter of police discretion.

title: Conjugal rights of a prisoner
explainer:
This case, decided by the Federal Shariat Court in 2010, dealt with the rights of prisoners to maintain family and conjugal relationships while incarcerated in Pakistan. The petitioner, Dr. Muhammad Aslam Khakhi, raised the issue in the context of prison rules and constitutional provisions relating to family life and dignity.

The court examined Rule 545-A of the Pakistan Prisons Rules, 1978, which allows prisoners special meetings with their spouses and children, calling it a positive and welcome development. The court held that spouses and children have a legitimate claim on prisoners to maintain family ties, and encouraged provincial Home Departments to formulate clear policies allowing married prisoners, excluding those sentenced to life imprisonment or death, to avail a week's parole every four months to preserve family life. It further suggested that for lifers and condemned prisoners, arrangements could be made for family reunions within special family quarters inside prison premises, since this could also help ease overcrowding and improve prisoner behavior.

The court directed all provincial governments and the federal Interior Secretary to review and strengthen these facilities, and to submit reports on the steps taken by the end of 2010, with a further review scheduled in 2011.

This judgment matters because it recognized that maintaining family bonds is an important human and constitutional right, even for those in custody, and pushed authorities to create structured, humane mechanisms for prisoners to stay connected with their families.

title: When benamidar is dismissed inheritance law is applicable
explainer:
This case concerns a property dispute filed in the Sindh High Court by a man, Din Muhammad Wagon, against his deceased wife's sister and her legal heirs. The plaintiff claimed that several properties, including houses, plots of land, gold ornaments, and cash held in a bank locker, were registered in his late wife Mst. Farkhanda Khatoon's name only as a formality (called a "benami" arrangement), while he was actually the true owner who had paid for everything using his own money. He asked the court to declare him the sole owner and to stop his wife's sister from claiming any share in these assets as an heir.

The court rejected the plaintiff's claim. It held that the burden was on him to prove the properties were bought with his own funds, but he failed to produce any documents or evidence showing he had paid for them. Since the properties were registered in his wife's name and he could not prove otherwise, the benami claim failed.

As a result, the properties were treated as belonging to the deceased wife herself. Since she died without children, Islamic inheritance law (Sunni Hanafi law) applied. The court ruled that both the husband and the deceased's sister were entitled to inherit shares of her estate, rejecting the plaintiff's attempt to claim everything for himself.

This case illustrates that mere registration of property in someone else's name isn't enough to prove a "benami" arrangement — solid proof of who actually paid for it is required, and inheritance laws take over when such claims fail.

The High Court dismissed her petition as filed too late, refusing to give her the benefit of Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, which allows extra time to be excluded when calculating deadlines in certain circumstances, such as delays in obtaining copies of judgments.

The Supreme Court took up her appeal specifically to decide whether this Limitation Act benefit applies to revision petitions filed under Section 115. The Court examined the history and purpose of Section 115, explaining that it gives the High Court supervisory power to correct jurisdictional errors and legal irregularities in lower courts, and should be exercised without undue technical obstacles. The Court traced amendments to Section 115 requiring subordinate courts to supply copies of decisions within three days, and set time limits for filing and deciding revisions, aimed at reducing delays in justice.

The Supreme Court found that the High Court had failed to check whether the lower court had actually complied with its duty to supply a copy of the judgment within the required three days, and if not, what consequences should follow. title: Order in Nawaz Sharif's Petition regarding Haqqani Case
explainer:
This is a Supreme Court of Pakistan order in the "Memogate" case, which arose from petitions filed by Nawaz Sharif and several other politicians, lawyers, and citizens after reports emerged of a secret memo allegedly sent to US Admiral Mike Mullen by Hussain Haqqani, Pakistan's then-Ambassador to the United States. The memo reportedly sought American help to rein in Pakistan's military and intelligence agencies, raising serious questions about national sovereignty and loyalty.

The Supreme Court had earlier set up a judicial commission, led by senior judges, to investigate the memo's origin, authenticity, and purpose. In this order, the Court received the commission's sealed report along with supporting evidence such as CDs, transcripts, phone records, and exhibits. The commission concluded that the memo was genuine and that Haqqani was its author and driving force. It found that Haqqani had acted disloyally by offering to help a foreign government gain influence over Pakistan's military, nuclear program, and intelligence services, and that this violated the Constitution. The Court ordered the findings to be made public and directed that copies be given to all parties, adjourning the case for two weeks. It also noted that Haqqani, who had left Pakistan, would need to respond to these findings.

This case matters because it dealt with serious allegations of an ambassador secretly undermining Pakistan's military establishment through a foreign power, touching on issues of sovereignty, civil-military relations, and accountability of public officials.

title: Misuse of authority by a Higher Official
explainer:
This case involved Ghani-ur-Rahman, who had served as Chairman of a District Council and later as a Provincial Minister in the former North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) accused him of misusing his official authority and accumulating assets—both in his own name and in the names of his wife and sons—that were disproportionate to his known sources of income, an offence under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999. He was convicted by an Accountability Court and sentenced to eight years imprisonment plus a heavy fine, with his family's assets ordered forfeited. The Peshawar High Court upheld this conviction, leading to his appeal before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him. It found that the prosecution had never actually determined or quantified his known sources of income, making it impossible to establish that his assets were "disproportionate." There was also no evidence of specific instances where he misused his authority. Crucially, his wife and sons, who were alleged to be holding assets on his behalf, were never even summoned by the trial court to explain their own resources—a serious procedural failure.

The judgment is significant because it highlights how incompetent investigation and prosecution, combined with courts failing to scrutinize basic legal requirements, can undermine corruption cases. The Supreme Court stressed that mere possession of assets is not a crime unless the prosecution proves those assets exceed a properly established income, and it criticized both NAB and the lower courts

title: Justice Rushed is Justice Crushed
explainer:
This case involved Wazir Ahmad, who was convicted by a Sessions Judge in Rajanpur for possessing 510 grams of charas under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, and sentenced to two years imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Lahore High Court, arguing that he had never been given a chance to hire a lawyer to defend him at trial, and was forced to cross-examine witnesses and argue his own case.

On reviewing the trial court's record, the High Court found this was true: the charge was framed without the appellant having legal representation, and on the very day the prosecution evidence was recorded, the trial court also heard his statement, took arguments, and delivered its final judgment, all in a single rushed sitting.

The High Court held that while speedy justice is a constitutional goal, it cannot come at the expense of the fundamental right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of one's choice, guaranteed under Article 10 of the Constitution. The court found the trial had moved with excessive haste, creating suspicion about its fairness. It set aside the conviction and sentence, and ordered a fresh trial from scratch, this time ensuring the appellant gets a real chance to engage a lawyer, and directed that the retrial be conducted by a different judge rather than the same Sessions Judge.

This case matters because it reinforces that fair process and the right to counsel cannot be sacrificed for speed, even when courts have good intentions.

title: Importance of Column 18 in case of Divorce
explainer:
This case, decided by the Islamabad court and reported as 2010 YLR 1632, dealt with a dispute between a husband, Ali Abbas Khan, and his wife, Mst. Palwasha Khan, over whether she had the legal right to divorce herself.

The wife claimed that column 18 of their Nikahnama (marriage contract), which mentioned certain "Shary Haqooq" (religious/legal rights), amounted to the husband delegating to her the power of Talaq-e-Tafweez, meaning the right to pronounce divorce on his behalf. Based on this claim, she sent a divorce deed to her husband and informed the Chairman of the Arbitration Council, who then issued a certificate confirming the divorce was effective.

The husband challenged this through a constitutional petition, arguing he never delegated any such power to his wife, that the general wording in column 18 did not amount to a specific delegation of divorce rights, and that the Arbitration Council had acted without lawful authority in certifying the divorce.

The court agreed with the husband. It held that a wife does not automatically have a religious or legal right to divorce herself unless the husband specifically and clearly delegates that power. General or vague wording in column 18 was not enough to establish such delegation. Since the husband denied giving this right, the court ruled the divorce deed had no legal effect and set aside the Arbitration Council's order.

title: Half conviction can be acquitted
explainer:
This case involved a man named Habibullah who was convicted by a trial court for two offenses: possessing explosives (hand grenades) under the Explosive Substances Act, and possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle under the Arms Ordinance. He was sentenced to five years for the explosives charge and three years for the weapons charge, to run together.

On appeal, the Peshawar High Court found serious problems with the explosives conviction. The law requires government sanction before prosecuting someone under the Explosive Substances Act, but no such sanction was ever presented as evidence at trial. Additionally, the report from the Bomb Disposal Unit was never formally introduced as evidence, and the appellant was never questioned about the recovered explosive materials when his statement was recorded, denying him a chance to explain himself. The investigation was also improperly conducted by a Head Constable who lacked the authority to investigate under Police Order 2002. For these reasons, the court set aside the explosives conviction entirely and acquitted him of that charge.

However, the court upheld his conviction for illegal possession of the Kalashnikov, since evidence for that recovery was solid, though it reduced his sentence to time already served.

This case matters because it shows how courts can partially overturn a conviction, acquitting on one charge while upholding another, based on procedural failures like missing legal sanctions and improper investigation, even when someone was convicted on multiple charges together.

title: Civil Revision dismissed in case of Benami
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Lahore between brothers. Muhammad Iqbal claimed that several properties, though purchased in his father Feroze Din's name, were actually bought with his own money as "benami" transactions, meaning his father was just holding the properties as a nominal owner while Iqbal was the true owner. Iqbal's father and brother, Muhammad Afzaal, disputed this, claiming the father genuinely owned the properties and had later gifted them to Afzaal.

The trial court and then the appellate court both ruled in favor of Iqbal after examining the evidence, agreeing that the properties were benami purchases and that Iqbal was the real owner. Afzaal then challenged these rulings before the Lahore High Court through a civil revision petition, arguing that Iqbal had failed to properly prove his income source and exclusive possession of the properties, and that family living arrangements meant income and possession should be considered joint.

The High Court dismissed the revision petition, upholding the concurrent findings of the two lower courts. It held that when two courts have already examined the facts and reached the same conclusion, a higher court exercising revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere just because it might have decided differently, unless there was a clear misreading of evidence. Since no such error was shown, the decisions favoring Iqbal stood. The case highlights how difficult it is to overturn matching factual findings of lower courts and clarifies principles around proving benami property transactions in Pakistani law.

title: Cancellation of plot due to delay in payment
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a farming cooperative society and the Capital Development Authority (CDA) over three plots of land in Islamabad that had been leased to the society in 1985 for agricultural use. The society had been paying for the land in installments and had invested heavily in developing the barren land into productive farmland growing fruits and vegetables. After paying seven installments without any problem, the society's eighth and final installment payment was rejected by CDA nine months after submission, on the grounds that it was late, and the plots were then cancelled without any prior notice or hearing.

The society challenged this cancellation through the courts for years, eventually reaching the Supreme Court after the Islamabad High Court dismissed its petition. The Supreme Court found that CDA had acted in bad faith. It could not explain why it sat on the payment for nine months before rejecting it, nor why it cancelled the plots without giving the society any notice or opportunity to be heard. The Court suspected CDA wanted to cancel the allotment so it could resell the now-improved land at a higher price due to rising property values. Since the society had already paid almost the entire cost and was only disputing minor delayed charges, and was willing to pay whatever remained due, the Supreme Court granted leave to appeal.

This case matters because it reinforces that government authorities cannot cancel citizens' property rights arbitrarily or without due process, even when technical defaults exist, especially when there are signs of bad faith or improper motives.

title: Writ Petition against order of Justice of Peace
explainer:
This case involved a murder investigation and a dispute over which version of events should be officially investigated by police.

A woman, Khalida Bibi, was murdered. Her husband, Liaqat Ali, registered an FIR (police report) naming certain accused persons, claiming she was killed over a demand for her agricultural land, and even produced a confessional statement from one accused implicating others. However, the victim's mother later filed an application before an Additional Sessions Judge, acting as Ex-officio Justice of Peace, alleging that the husband himself, in collusion with police, had engineered this FIR to protect himself and the real killers, and that he and his associates were actually responsible for her daughter's murder. The Justice of Peace directed police to record the mother's version and investigate further.

The husband challenged this order in the Lahore High Court, arguing that once an FIR exists for an occurrence, a second FIR for the same incident cannot be registered.

The High Court disagreed and dismissed the petition. It found the husband's conduct suspicious, noting he had taken "meticulous precautions" by engineering a confession from another accused in a case that seemed to rely on direct eyewitness evidence, raising doubts about that statement's legitimacy. Since the mother's application presented an entirely different version of events implicating the husband himself, the court held it was lawful to record a second FIR in these circumstances, relying on precedent permitting this in appropriate cases.

This case matters because it clarifies that a second FIR can be registered when it presents a genuinely different account of a crime, particular

title: Wife can claim maintenance even living seperately
explainer:
This case involved a wife, Mst. Gulsheeda Bibi, who sought dissolution of her marriage through khula (a wife's right to end a marriage), along with recovery of her dower, dowry articles, and maintenance for herself and her minor daughter. She alleged that after living happily with her husband for about a year and three months, he began mistreating her, beating and abusing her, and took away jewelry given to her at marriage. The husband denied this and filed his own suit demanding restitution of conjugal rights, claiming she left without good reason.

The Family Court had ruled in the wife's favor on all counts, granting khula, dowry recovery, and maintenance, while dismissing the husband's suit. He appealed.

The Azad Jammu & Kashmir High Court upheld the khula, explaining that such a decree is proper when the court is satisfied the spouses have developed such hatred and mistrust that reconciliation is impossible, since forcing a hateful union to continue serves no purpose. On dowry, the court reduced the amount awarded from Rs. 150,000 to Rs. 100,000, accounting for items destroyed in an earthquake and items still with the husband. Importantly, the court clarified that a wife who has valid reasons for living apart—such as cruelty or non-payment of dower—can still claim maintenance, even without returning to her husband. Only a wife who refuses to live with her husband without justification loses that right. This clarifies protections for wives who leave abusive or neglectful marriages.

title: Suit dismissed under order 7 rule 11
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over money allegedly owed based on a handwritten note in the margin of a legal agreement. Respondent No. 1 had mortgaged his shop to Respondent No. 2 to secure a loan. Later, the two settled their dispute through an agreement dated 2-1-2001, which cancelled the mortgage after Respondent No. 1 paid Rs. 100,000, with both sides agreeing that nothing further was owed. However, a note in the margin of that agreement, allegedly signed by the petitioner (who was separately buying the shop from Respondent No. 1), suggested he had made the payment and would recover certain items and money from Respondent No. 2. Based on this note, Respondent No. 1 sued the petitioner for recovery. The trial court dismissed the suit, but the appellate court reversed this and ruled in favor of Respondent No. 1.

The High Court, hearing a revision petition, found that the note did not qualify as a valid or enforceable guarantee. It lacked proper parties, clear terms, consideration, and was inconsistent with the main settlement agreement stating nothing further was due. A separate second agreement between the original parties also had no legal bearing on the petitioner, who was not part of it. Since there was no valid basis for the claim, the court held that Respondent No. 1 had no legal cause of action.

The court set aside the lower courts' decisions and rejected the suit entirely, showing how vague, informal notes cannot substitute for legally binding agreements.

title: Status of Arbitration in family suits
explainer:
This Supreme Court judgment dealt with a family dispute between a wife (Farzana Rasool and others) and her husband, Dr. Muhammad Bashir. The wife had filed two suits at the Family Court - one for return of her dowry articles and another for maintenance for herself and her children. While these cases were pending, and while the husband had also filed an application to transfer the case to another court, he voluntarily agreed, on oath before the District Judge, to let a panel of advocates he himself chose resolve all matrimonial disputes, promising their decision would be binding on him. The panel gave its findings, and the Family Court used them to decide in the wife's favor. The husband later objected, but his appeals were rejected until the High Court sided with him, ruling that arbitration procedures were not applicable in family court cases and setting aside the decision.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court and restored the original judgment favoring the wife. It held that nothing stops parties in family cases from choosing mediation or arbitration to settle their disputes, especially when it reflects the Islamic principle of amicable dispute resolution encouraged under the Family Courts Act. Since the husband himself had proposed and agreed to this process, he could not later object. The Court emphasized that family law procedures are meant to be simple, quick, and free of rigid technicalities, and that courts should actively encourage compromise between spouses. This ruling clarifies that voluntary arbitration agreements between spouses in family cases are valid and enforceable.

title: Power of court to issue summons on application
explainer:
This case involved three pre-emption lawsuits filed by the petitioner, which had been ongoing for several years while he tried to present his witnesses in court. Despite repeated adjournments, delays caused by court officials being unavailable, and witnesses actually showing up on some dates, the trial court eventually closed his right to present evidence and dismissed his suits after one witness failed to appear on a particular date.

The Lahore High Court found that the trial court had acted unfairly. It noted that two of the petitioner's witnesses were present and ready to testify, but the case was still adjourned simply because a third witness--who had been summoned through the court itself--could not be located. The court held that once a judge decides to issue summons directly (rather than requiring the party to arrange it), the court has a legal duty to ensure the summons was properly served according to procedure. Since the petitioner had been actively producing witnesses and cooperating throughout, his conduct was not deliberately obstructive or defiant. The trial court had wrongly placed the entire burden on him to secure the missing witness's appearance.

As a result, the High Court set aside the dismissal and sent the cases back to the trial court, ruling that the petitioner deserved one more fair opportunity to complete his evidence. This decision matters because it reinforces that courts must not penalize litigants for delays caused by the court's own procedural failures, and that any restriction on producing evidence must be applied fairly and only when a party is genuinely at fault.

title: Petitioners should be given chance of hearing
explainer:
This case arose from a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell land, filed by Muhammad Usman against Major Pervez Shakoor and four others. When the defendants failed to appear, the suit was decided against them ex-parte. They applied to have that ex-parte decree set aside, but this application itself was later dismissed for non-prosecution because they again failed to appear. They then filed a further application seeking restoration of their original application, explaining that they lived in Karachi and were unaware of the hearing date, and that their lawyer was occupied with election-related work at the time, so their absence was unintentional.

The trial court rejected this restoration application without framing any issue or giving the petitioners a chance to prove their explanation, and the appellate court upheld this decision. The petitioners then approached the Lahore High Court.

The High Court held that the petitioners had provided reasons for their non-appearance and were entitled to a proper opportunity to prove those reasons through evidence. Since no issue was framed and no such opportunity was given, the rejection of their application was arbitrary and could not be upheld.

The court accepted the petition, set aside the lower courts' orders, and sent the case back to the trial court to decide the restoration application afresh, after framing issues and letting both sides present evidence. This case highlights the basic fairness principle that litigants must be heard before being penalized.

title: Khulah cannot be stopped if haq mehar is not returned
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with disputes over dissolution of marriage through khula (a wife's right to seek divorce by returning consideration received from her husband) under the West Pakistan Muslim Family Courts Act, 1964. The husband challenged a Family Court's decision granting his wife a khula decree, apparently arguing that the divorce should not take effect unless the dower (haq mehar) issue was fully resolved first.

The High Court ruled that a Family Court cannot delay or refuse to grant a khula decree simply because the spouses disagree over whether the dower has been paid or returned. It explained that the law was designed to give wives fast relief through khula, since lengthy trials in the past often made divorce decrees meaningless by the time they were issued. The Court held that when reconciliation fails, the Family Court should grant the khula decree immediately, while separately determining—if contested—how much dower money the wife may need to return to the husband afterward. The divorce takes effect from the date it is pronounced, regardless of the dower dispute.

The Court also stressed that judges must make genuine, documented efforts at reconciliation before granting khula, criticizing the trial judge for not properly recording such efforts. This judgment matters because it protects women's ability to exit unwanted marriages quickly through khula, while balancing the husband's right to reclaim dower through separate proceedings, and reinforces the importance of genuine reconciliation efforts in family disputes.

title: Importance of column 16 of Nikah Nama
explainer:
This case is about a wife's claim for her dower (mehr) under a Nikah Nama, the Islamic marriage contract that records the terms agreed between spouses at marriage. The wife had sued for recovery of dower, maintenance, dowry articles, and dissolution of marriage. The Family Court initially decreed in her favor as claimed. On appeal, the Additional District Judge reduced her entitlement to only Rs. 50,000, the amount written in Column 13 of the Nikah Nama as the fixed dower.

The wife challenged this before the Peshawar High Court, arguing the appellate court misread Columns 13, 14, and 16, which also mentioned eight tolas of gold ornaments and referenced a five-marla plot of land.

The High Court held that Nikah Nama columns must be read together and interpreted according to their plain, ordinary meaning, since Nikah Nama carries strong legal presumption of truth like a registered document. It found that Column 14 clearly showed eight tolas of gold were promised as dower alongside the cash amount, and since this was never paid nor challenged, the wife was entitled to it in addition to Rs. 50,000. However, it ruled that Column 16, about immovable property, did not create a separate independent right since the plot had no specified boundaries or details, so it could not be treated as additional property owed.

The petition was partly accepted, modifying the dower amount to Rs. 50,000 plus the gold ornaments or their market value. The case clarifies how courts should interpret Nikah Nama entries

title: How to prove a person is shia
explainer:
This case was about a family property dispute that turned on a person's religious sect. After Sardar Fazal Khan died, his property passed to his two daughters through an inheritance mutation registered under Shia law. Some of his relatives (collaterals) then sued, claiming a share of the property on the grounds that Fazal Khan was actually Sunni, which would make the Shia inheritance mutation invalid.

The trial court dismissed the relatives' suit, but the appellate court and later the High Court sided with them, deciding the mutation was wrongful. The daughters then approached the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court examined the evidence on how to determine someone's actual faith after death. It ruled that having a Sunni cleric lead the funeral prayers proves nothing about the deceased's true beliefs, since the deceased has no control over how others choose to bury them, and the choice of who leads the prayer belongs to the living, not the dead. Instead, the Court found more reliable evidence in the fact that close relatives on both sides were Shia, that a Shia cleric had also led funeral prayers, and importantly, that the deceased used to fly the Alam (flag) of Hazrat Abbas at his house, a practice strongly associated with Shia faith.

Based on this, the Supreme Court concluded Fazal Khan was Shia, overturned the lower courts, and restored the original decision favoring the daughters. The case is significant for establishing that religious identity in inheritance disputes should be judged by lifestyle practices and community ties rather than funeral ritu

title: Ground of cross case should be taken on time
explainer:
This case involved Arif, who was accused of firing at a man named Muhammad Fayaz along with his brother and father. His first bail application was rejected by the Peshawar High Court on merits. He then filed a second bail application, arguing that since his co-accused Waris (his father) had since been granted bail based on the existence of a cross case—an FIR filed by Waris's wife accusing the original complainant of injuring Waris and another person—Arif should also get bail on the same ground, or at least under the principle of consistency (treating similarly situated co-accused alike).

The court examined whether this cross-case argument was genuinely a fresh ground. It found that the existence of the cross case was already on record and had even been referenced in an earlier court order concerning Arif's first bail application, but his lawyer had not raised or pressed it at that time. The court held that a ground that existed but was simply overlooked or not argued earlier cannot later be treated as a fresh ground, especially since ignorance of the record isn't a valid excuse.

The court also rejected the consistency argument, since Waris, unlike Arif, was himself injured in the cross case—making their situations different. Therefore, Arif's bail application was dismissed. The case highlights that bail arguments must be raised promptly, not recycled later as "new" grounds.

title: Execution can be adjourned sine die
explainer:
This case is about a company, Quice Food Industries Limited, and its directors who had taken loans from a bank and later defaulted. The bank won a court decree against them and began execution proceedings to recover the money. However, the company and bank later reached a settlement, restructuring the debt into a new repayment schedule of installments. The execution court accepted this compromise and put the execution proceedings on hold indefinitely (sine die), allowing the company to pay according to the new agreement.

Separately, the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) had filed a reference against the company's directors for wilful default under accountability laws. Even though the bank confirmed the company was making regular payments under the new agreement, the Accountability Court refused to dismiss the case, saying evidence was still needed.

The Sindh High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that the new restructuring agreement replaced (novated) the original loan agreement, meaning the old obligations no longer applied. Since the company was paying regularly under the new agreement, it could not be said to be in wilful default. The court stayed the Accountability Court proceedings and ordered them quashed if full payment was made under the new agreement, though NAB could ask to revive the case if the company failed to pay.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that when banks and debtors formally restructure loans, courts should recognize the new agreement's terms in assessing default, rather than relying solely on the original loan terms.

title: Contract Employees Appointment Case in Punjab
explainer:
This case involved secretaries of Union Councils in Punjab who had been appointed on a contract basis in 2007, when the required qualification was Matriculation (at least second division). Later, the government issued notifications allowing contract employees to be made regular, subject to certain service rules. However, in 2005, the qualification requirement for this post was raised to F.A. (a higher qualification), effective from 2007 onward. Some contract employees who met the new, higher qualification were regularized, but those who only had the original Matric qualification, like the petitioners, were denied regularization.

The petitioners challenged this before the court, arguing that their eligibility should be judged based on the qualification required at the time they were originally appointed, not a later, stricter standard. The court agreed. It held that since Matriculation was the valid qualification when the petitioners joined, they could not be denied regularization simply because a new rule later demanded higher qualifications. The 2005 amendment could not be applied retrospectively to disadvantage employees who were already serving under the old rules.

As a result, the court set aside the earlier order denying regularization and ruled that all petitioners who met the qualification requirements applicable on their date of initial appointment should have their services regularized.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that changes in job qualification requirements cannot be used retroactively to deny rights or benefits to employees who were lawfully appointed under earlier, valid rules.

title: Childless widow is entitled for share in movable property
explainer:
This case concerns a widow's right to inherit property from her deceased husband when the couple had no children, and involved a dispute over which Islamic sect the husband belonged to, since Sunni and Shia inheritance rules differ on this point.

The widow, Ayesha Bibi, sued for a declaration that she was entitled to inherit her late husband Muhammad Khan's land and other property. She argued he was a Sunni Muslim, so she should inherit normally. Her stepson, Nazar Muhammad, opposed this, claiming his father was actually a Shia Muslim, and under Shia (Fiqh Jafria) law, a childless widow is excluded from inheriting agricultural land. The trial court sided with the son and dismissed the widow's suit, but the appellate court reversed this and ruled in her favor, prompting the son to challenge that decision before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court examined authoritative texts on Muhammadan law and clarified an important legal point: even under Shia jurisprudence, a childless widow's exclusion applies only to landed property (agricultural land). She remains entitled to a share in all other movable assets of her husband's estate, such as buildings, trees, household items, tube-wells, animals, and other personal property.

Because the lower courts had not properly examined the case with this distinction in mind, the High Court sent the case back for fresh determination, ensuring the widow's rightful claim to movable property would be properly assessed regardless of the sectarian inheritance dispute over the land.
