# Case Explainer: Muhammad Yaqub v. Master Muhammad Shafi

**What was this case about?**

This was a landlord-tenant dispute over a house in Quetta. Under rent law, once eviction proceedings begin, the Rent Controller can order a tenant to keep depositing rent regularly. If the tenant fails to pay on time, the landlord can ask the court to "strike off" (cancel) the tenant's defence, which effectively leads to eviction.

Here, the tenant missed depositing rent for June 1980. The landlord found out and applied over a year later to have the tenant's defence struck off. The tenant argued that this long delay meant the landlord had "waived" (given up) his right to object, and separately claimed he was seriously ill when the delay occurred.

**What did the court decide?**

The court found the tenant had acted deceptively — depositing rent through court challans (receipts) without mentioning which month it was for, and even erasing/altering details to hide the missed payment. Because the landlord didn't know about the default earlier, he could not be said to have knowingly waived his right — waiver requires knowledge of a right and a deliberate decision to give it up. The illness excuse was also rejected as an afterthought, since it wasn't raised when the tenant first tendered the late rent.

The court upheld the order striking off the tenant's defence and eviction.

title: Power of a family court in khula cases
explainer:
This case involves a wife, Dr. Nosheen Qamar, who sued for dissolution of her marriage on grounds including cruelty, non-payment of maintenance, and her husband taking a second wife without her consent. She also claimed dower (money and property promised to her at marriage) worth Rs. 200,000 plus gold ornaments and a house share. The trial court dissolved the marriage but didn't clearly state whether it was granting a "khula" (wife-initiated divorce, which under Islamic law can require the wife to give up her dower). The husband later argued in the High Court that since it was effectively a khula, his wife should forfeit her right to the dower money—and the High Court agreed, denying her the Rs. 200,000.

The Supreme Court, in this order, granted leave to appeal, meaning it agreed to seriously review the case rather than reject it. The Court raised several important legal questions: whether the trial court's findings actually supported a khula ruling, whether dower is automatically forfeited in a khula divorce, whether the wife could still defend her case even if she hadn't formally appealed one specific finding, and whether the High Court could decide on the dower issue at all while a related appeal was already pending elsewhere.

This case matters because it addresses how courts should determine whether a divorce counts as khula, and whether women automatically lose financial rights (like dower) in such cases—an issue affecting family law rights across Pakistan.

title: Time period for restoring suit dismissed in default
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute where a father (Sikandar Ali) was seeking to overturn an ex-parte (one-sided) custody decree granted to the mother (Robina Kousar) for their minor child.

Background: A custody decree was issued against the father on 18.3.2004 without his participation. He later filed a petition to set this aside, but that petition was dismissed for non-prosecution (failure to pursue the case) on 5.1.2005. An earlier attempt to restore that petition had already failed. He then filed another restoration application on 10.6.2005 — over five months after the dismissal — claiming his junior lawyer had misunderstood which cases were scheduled for hearing.

The Court's Decision: The AJ&K High Court upheld the lower court's dismissal. Under Rule XII(II) of the Family Court Procedural Rules, 1998, a court can restore a case dismissed for default only if the restoration application is filed within 30 days and shows sufficient cause. Here, the father's application came five months late, with no explanation for the delay and no application to excuse it. His claim about his lawyer's confusion was unsupported by any affidavit. The Court also noted his own petition admitted an earlier restoration attempt had already failed and become final.

Why it matters: This case confirms that strict time limits apply to restoring dismissed cases in family court, and that vague excuses without evidence (like affidavits) or formal delay-condonation requests won't succeed—even in sensitive matters like child custody.

**What was this case about?**

A husband (Dr. Ejaz Naseem) filed a case for restitution of conjugal rights against his wife (Fareeha Ahmad). In response, the wife filed a written statement seeking divorce through khula, plus recovery of money, jewelry, household goods, maintenance for herself and her two daughters, and educational/maternity expenses. Before evidence was recorded, both parties reached a compromise, and the Family Court passed a decree in 2005 based on that agreement—granting divorce and the wife's other claims.

Later, when the wife tried to enforce (execute) this decree, the husband objected, then appealed—390 days late. He argued that the Family Court never had the legal power (jurisdiction) to decide claims like money, jewelry, and expenses based on a written statement; only khula could be claimed that way, and consent between parties cannot create jurisdiction that the law doesn't provide.

**What did the Supreme Court decide?**

The Court rejected his argument. It held that Section 5 of the Family Courts Act gives Family Courts exclusive jurisdiction over all matters listed in the Act's Schedule—including divorce, dower, maintenance, custody, dowry, and personal property—regardless of whether they're raised as claims or counter-claims. Since the husband never objected to jurisdiction earlier and had voluntarily agreed to the compromise, he was estopped (legally barred) from challenging it now. His 390-day-late appeal was also rightly rejected.

title: Ingredients of a Benami Transactions
explainer:
**Case Summary: Benami Transaction Dispute**

This case involved a property dispute between Qurib Ali and his brother's family (respondents) over land that was officially registered in the name of Qurib Ali's brother, Muhammad Chuttal.

**Background:** Qurib Ali worked for the former Khairpur State government. During his employment, government rules barred civil servants from purchasing land in their own names without permission. To get around this restriction, he bought land but registered it in his brother's name—this is called a "benami" transaction, where the person who actually pays for and owns property registers it under someone else's name.

Qurib Ali claimed he paid the full purchase price, kept possession of the land, held the original title documents, and paid all government taxes on the property. After being forcibly removed from the land, he sued to be recognized as the true owner. Both the trial court and the High Court initially rejected his claim, saying he lacked sufficient documentary proof.

**Supreme Court's Intervention:** The Supreme Court sent the case back, clarifying that documentary evidence isn't always necessary to prove a benami transaction—courts should look at the whole picture.

**Final Decision:** On review, the High Court ruled in Qurib Ali's favor. It found that the source of payment, possession of documents, physical possession of the land, and his motive (avoiding the government service ban) all proved he was the real owner. The Court restored his ownership and ordered compensation for lost profits.

**Why it matters:** This case clarifies the legal test for identifying benami transactions

title: When a child is legal?
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A man (the petitioner) was ordered by a Family Court to pay maintenance (financial support) to two children. He challenged this order in the Lahore High Court, denying that he was the father of the minors. He claimed the children were actually born from the mother's previous husband, not from him.

**What did the court find?**

The High Court examined the evidence and found that the man and woman had lived together as husband and wife, and the children were born during this cohabitation. The woman had consistently maintained that she was his legally wedded wife. Importantly, the man never filed a legal case (called a "suit for jactitation of marriage") to formally dispute or disprove her claim of marriage — something he could have done if he genuinely believed the marriage wasn't valid. The court also noted that he had previously sent maintenance money for the children through money order while they lived in another city, which contradicted his denial of paternity.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court ruled that the children were legitimate offspring of the man, born from a lawful marital union. It dismissed his petition, upheld the maintenance order, and even imposed additional costs on him — criticizing his conduct as "shameful" for trying to avoid his legal and moral duty to support his own children.

**Why it matters:**

This case shows how courts determine a child's legitimacy using evidence of cohabitation and marital status, and reinforces that fathers cannot evade financial responsibility for their children through denial alone.

title: NEPRA REGULATIONS, 2012
explainer:
This is not a court judgment—it is a set of procedural regulations (subordinate legislation) issued by Pakistan's National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA) in 2012, under powers granted by the Regulation of Generation, Transmission and Distribution of Electric Power Act, 1997.

The regulations establish the process for filing appeals before NEPRA against decisions of a single Member of the Authority, the Tribunal, or a Provincial Inspection office. Key rules include: appeals must be filed within 30 days of the order (with provision for delay if there's sufficient cause); appeals must be sent by registered post or courier to the Registrar, accompanied by a verified affidavit, a certified copy of the challenged order, and a Rs. 1,000 fee; documents must be typed, paginated, and submitted in four sets. The regulations also detail how the Registrar screens appeals for defects, how notice is given to the opposing party (respondent), how respondents may reply within 10 days, and how hearings and adjournments are handled—including dismissal of an appeal if the appellant doesn't show up, subject to restoration on valid grounds.

This matters because it creates a clear, standardized procedure for consumers, licensees, or other affected parties to challenge electricity-related regulatory decisions, ensuring fairness, transparency, and timely resolution of disputes within Pakistan's electric power regulatory system. # Can a Government Employee Break a Scholarship Bond to Take a University Job?

**What the case was about:**

This case involved a man convicted by a trial court for an offence related to zina (unlawful sexual relations) under Pakistan's Hudood Ordinance. The trial court convicted him under Section 10(2) of the Zina Ordinance and sentenced him to seven years in prison plus a fine.

The court also noted suspicious conduct by witnesses and missing evidentiary links.

Because the abduction element wasn't proven and evidence of marriage created reasonable doubt, the court gave the accused the benefit of the doubt and accepted his appeal, meaning his conviction was overturned.

title: No person can have favorite portion in joint property without consent of others
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A group of relatives (respondents) who were recorded as co-owners in revenue records filed a suit demanding possession of their share in jointly-owned property through partition. The petitioners, who were in possession of the land, contested this. Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in favor of the respondents, confirming their ownership shares and ordering partition. The petitioners then challenged these decisions before the Peshawar High Court, arguing that not all co-owners were made parties to the suit and that the courts had ignored evidence and legal objections they had raised.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that the revenue records clearly showed the respondents as co-owners, and the petitioners never disputed this in their pleadings or claimed sole ownership of the property. Since parties cannot argue points at trial that weren't raised in their pleadings, this objection failed. The court also clarified that while a preliminary decree for partition was rightly passed, all co-owners must eventually be joined before a final decree distributing specific plots is issued.

**Why does it matter?**

The judgment reinforces a key principle of property law: no co-owner can unilaterally occupy or claim a specific, favorable portion of jointly-owned land just because of informal family arrangements or long-standing possession. Without the consent of all co-owners and proper legal partition proceedings, such arrangements don't create ownership rights. This protects the equal rights of all co-owners in shared property.

This case arose from a false criminal accusation. A man named Muhammad Saeed and a woman, Mst. Zarin Khatoon, had married each other by their own consent. However, some relatives of the woman filed a police case claiming Saeed and others had forcibly abducted her, invoking the harsh Zina (Enforcement of Hadood) Ordinance, 1979 — a charge carrying life imprisonment.

The trial court acquitted the accused, giving them the benefit of the doubt. When the case reached the Federal Shariat Court on appeal, the Court found overwhelming evidence that Zarin Khatoon and Saeed had genuinely married and lived as husband and wife months before the alleged "abduction" date. The witnesses who claimed abduction had given self-contradictory and knowingly false statements to fabricate a case against multiple innocent people, including even the cleric who performed the marriage.

The Court held that producing a formal marriage certificate (Nikahnama) isn't essential to prove marriage — the couple's own consistent claim of being husband and wife is enough. More importantly, it ruled that deliberately fabricating false abduction allegations amounts to perjury and fabricating evidence under the Pakistan Penal Code (Sections 193 and 195), especially serious because it sought to send innocent people to prison for life on a false charge.

As a result, three of the false witnesses were convicted of perjury and sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment each.

title: Powers to Conduct Audit
explainer:
Laraib Energy Limited, a company operating a hydroelectric power complex, challenged notices issued by tax officers (Commissioner and Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue) asking it to produce records for an audit of its sales tax and federal excise affairs. The company argued that only the Board of Revenue—not the Commissioner—had the power under Section 72B of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, to select taxpayers for audit. It relied on a Lahore High Court ruling supporting this view.

The tax authorities countered that Section 25 of the same Act separately empowered the Commissioner and Inland Revenue officers to access records and conduct audits, independent of the Board's selection power under Section 72B. They pointed to a clarifying "Explanation" added to the law and a similar case from the Islamabad High Court that upheld such notices.

The Azad Jammu & Kashmir High Court agreed with the tax authorities. It held that the Commissioner's power under Section 25 (and similarly under the Income Tax Ordinance) to call for records and conduct audits is separate from the Board's power under Section 72B. The Court reasoned that self-assessment by taxpayers isn't beyond verification, and tax laws shouldn't be interpreted to add restrictions not clearly stated. Finding no merit in the company's arguments, the Court dismissed the petition outright.

This case matters because it clarifies that tax officers can independently exercise audit powers without needing prior selection by the central Board of Revenue.

title: Quashment in a Drugs Act 1976 case
explainer:
**What the case was about:**

This case involved two employees of a pharmaceutical company (a Quality Control Incharge and a Warrantor) who were being prosecuted under Pakistan's Drugs Act, 1976, after a drug sample (Renuvit capsules) was found to be "substandard and misbranded" by a government laboratory. The accused had asked the trial court (Drug Court, Balochistan) to dismiss the case against them before trial, but their request was rejected. They then approached the High Court seeking to have the entire case quashed.

**What the court decided:**

The Balochistan High Court accepted the petition and quashed the proceedings, for two main reasons:

1. **The company itself was never prosecuted** — only its employees were. Citing Supreme Court precedent, the court held that employees cannot be held liable unless the company is first found guilty; since the company wasn't even a party to the case, this was fatal to the prosecution.

2. **The lab report was dangerously late.** The law requires analysis reports within 60 days, with any delay formally justified in writing. Here, the report took over nine months, with no explanation given. The court called this a violation of a "mandatory" legal requirement, meaning no conviction could be based on it.

**Why it matters:**

The ruling reinforces that procedural safeguards under the Drugs Act—like timely testing and proper accountability of companies before their employees—must be strictly followed. Courts can quash cases early if there's no realistic chance of conviction, sparing accused persons from pointless trials.

explainer:
This case is about a long-running dispute over a petrol pump/CNG station site in Islamabad, leased by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) through its Staff Welfare Organization to Mr. S.M. Ismail in 1973 for 30 years.

When the lease neared its end, CDA offered only a 5-year extension at a much higher rent. Ismail didn't reject this outright but instead asked for a full 30-year renewal, similar to what CDA itself enjoyed. Instead of responding properly, CDA later forcibly dispossessed him and sealed his premises without following proper legal procedure or giving prior notice.

The Lahore High Court (Rawalpindi Bench) ruled that:

1. Ismail's petition to the High Court was valid, since he was dispossessed without required legal notice.
2. Government bodies must act fairly and lawfully, and courts can step in when they don't.
3. Since this was a lease (not a rent-controlled tenancy), the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction — this was a landlord-tenant lease matter, not one covered by rent laws.
4. CDA's dispossession of Ismail was illegal and done in bad faith ("arrogant" and "malicious"), especially since CDA itself benefited from long renewable leases but denied the same fairness to Ismail.

The Court ordered Ismail's possession restored and directed CDA to extend his lease for another 30 years, applying principles of equity and fairness.

title: Technicalities would be avoided and matter would be decided on Merit
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over maintenance (financial support) payments in Multan. The wife had sued her husband for maintenance for herself and their four children (two daughters and two sons). When the husband stopped participating in the case, the court passed an ex-parte (one-sided) decree against him, ordering him to pay maintenance for all four children and his wife.

The husband filed an application to set aside this ex-parte decree, and evidence was actually recorded in his favor. However, he later missed a hearing, and his application was dismissed for "non-prosecution" (failure to pursue the case) rather than being decided on its actual merits. When he asked the court to restore his application, that request was also rejected. An appeal to a higher court also failed.

The Lahore High Court found this troubling, especially since the two adult sons appeared in court supporting their father, claiming they had been living with him all along—meaning their mother may have wrongly claimed maintenance for them.

The High Court ruled that cases should be decided on their merits (the actual facts and evidence) rather than dismissed on technical grounds like missed appearances. It set aside the lower courts' rulings and ordered the case to be reconsidered properly, with evidence examined, within two months—though the husband first had to pay any overdue maintenance for the daughters.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts should prioritize fair, evidence-based decisions over rigid procedural technicalities.

Two men (Muhammad Ramzan and another) were named in a police case (FIR) accusing them of dacoity (armed robbery) under Section 392 of the Pakistan Penal Code. title: Procedure when defendant is in Jail
explainer:
Here's a plain-language explainer:

**What the case was about:**
Muhammad Nazir sued Shafqat Mehmood to recover Rs. 38,80,000 based on a cheque, using a special fast-track court procedure (Order XXXVII CPC) for cheque-recovery cases. At the time the suit was filed, Mehmood was in jail on an unrelated criminal case. The court tried to serve him legal notice through the jail superintendent, but this failed, so the court eventually resorted to publishing a public notice in a newspaper. A lawyer then filed papers on Mehmood's behalf seeking permission to defend the suit — but the trial court rejected this application, ruling it was filed too late (after the 10-day legal deadline).

**What the court decided:**
The Lahore High Court disagreed. It found that Mehmood was never properly served according to law while he was in jail — publishing a newspaper notice for someone in custody was impractical and improper. Since proper service never happened, the 10-day clock for responding hadn't actually started running. The court ruled that when someone is in jail, the law requires proper steps (like producing him from jail for service) — skipping these isn't a mere technicality but a real legal failure. The petition was accepted, meaning Mehmood's request to defend himself would go forward.

**Why it matters:**
This case reinforces that courts must follow proper service procedures, especially for jailed defendants, and should prioritize real justice over rigid technical dismissals when someone was unable to respond through no fault of their own.

title: Theft case Bail Granted after Partial Recovery
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Six men (Muhammad Madni and others) were accused of stealing two buffaloes, two calves, and two cows belonging to a complainant. A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against them under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with theft (Section 380), giving false information to mislead an investigation (Section 215), and dishonestly receiving stolen property (Section 411). The police claimed to have recovered one buffalo and one calf from the accused. The men had been in jail since July 2013 and sought "post-arrest bail" — meaning release while their trial proceeds.

**What did the court decide?**

The Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) granted them bail. The judge noted that although police claimed a recovery of animals, the recovery memo showed it was a "joint recovery" — meaning the property was recovered from multiple accused together rather than pinpointed to a specific individual through their own disclosure. Courts generally consider such joint recoveries weak evidence, as they don't clearly establish which specific accused led police to the stolen goods. The court also noted the alleged offense wasn't among the serious crimes barred from bail under Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

**Why does it matter?**

This case illustrates an important legal principle: recovery evidence attributed jointly to several accused, rather than individually, carries little weight in Pakistani courts. It also shows how bail is often granted for offenses not classified as most serious, especially when evidence against the accused appears weak.

# Case Explainer: Amjad Ali and Others v. Anwar Shah and Others (PLJ 2015)

**What was this case about?**

This dispute centered on a house in Peshawar. The original plaintiff, Khalil Khan, claimed he owned the house and that Haji Yar Badshah was his tenant who paid rent (called "Khak Shora"). Khalil Khan filed a lawsuit to evict Yar Badshah and take possession of the property.

However, the situation became complicated. Yar Badshah had earlier filed his own lawsuit claiming he owned the property through "adverse possession" (a legal claim based on long-term occupation), but that suit was dismissed. After Yar Badshah died, his sons (the respondents) were brought into the case as his legal heirs. But they also claimed a *separate* right to the property—they said they had independently purchased shares in it through official land mutations and a registered sale deed, making them co-owners, not just tenants' heirs.

**What did the Court decide?**

The Peshawar High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the lower appellate court's decision to reject the eviction claim. The plaintiff failed to prove: (1) that a landlord-tenant relationship actually existed, (2) which specific portion of the property was being rented, and (3) that rent payments were ever made. The Court also noted the respondents had legitimately purchased ownership shares *before* the eviction suit was even filed.

**Why does this matter?**

The judgment clarifies that tenancy rights don't

automatically transfer or apply to someone's legal heirs if those heirs can independently prove they hold a separate, legitimate ownership interest in the same property—especially when that ownership was acquired through documented, verified means (like registered sale deeds) prior to the litigation. It reinforces the principle that a plaintiff seeking eviction bears the burden of proving all essential elements of the landlord-tenant relationship, including the specific rented premises and actual rent payments; unsubstantiated claims cannot succeed merely because the opposing party was originally brought into a case as legal heirs of a deceased litigant.

title: 2005 M L D 834
explainer:
This case involves a family dispute over property. The respondent (a woman) had filed a partition suit, claiming a share in property presumably as a widow. The petitioner, in her written statement responding to the suit, argued that the respondent had actually been divorced by her husband before his death, by mutual consent—meaning she would have no claim to inherit as a widow. Faced with this claim, the respondent withdrew her partition suit rather than contest it.

The petitioner then went further: she asked the trial court to initiate criminal proceedings against the respondent under Section 476 of the Criminal Procedure Code, arguing that the respondent had lied to the court by falsely claiming to be the deceased's widow in order to get a share of the property.

Both the trial court and the appellate court refused to initiate such proceedings. The petitioner then approached the High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution, asking it to overturn these refusals.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It explained that Section 476 uses the word "may," meaning courts have discretion whether to prosecute someone for making a false claim—it's not mandatory. Since the lower courts had already exercised this discretion (choosing not to prosecute) based on the case's circumstances, the High Court said it could not simply substitute its own opinion for theirs under its constitutional writ powers.

This case matters because it clarifies that courts have discretionary power in such matters, and higher courts should respect that discretion rather than freely overturning it.

explainer:
This case involved five people—Muhammad Javed, Raheem Zada, Abdul Hameed, Mst. Tabassam, and Nawaz Khan—who were convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Multan for kidnapping a young man, Usman Ahmad, and demanding one crore rupees in ransom from his father, Bashir Ahmad. All five were sentenced to life imprisonment under Section 365-A of the Pakistan Penal Code (kidnapping for ransom) and Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act. They appealed their convictions, while the complainant filed a separate petition asking that their sentences be increased to the death penalty.

The Lahore High Court's Multan Bench overturned the convictions and acquitted all the appellants. The judges found the prosecution's case full of serious doubts: there was confusion over where the abduction actually took place, no witness had seen the victim with the accused, the complainant couldn't identify who had negotiated the ransom over the phone, and the victim gave only vague details about where he was held captive.

The court relied on a well-established legal principle: in criminal cases, if there's even one significant circumstance that creates reasonable doubt about an accused's guilt, they must be given the "benefit of the doubt" and acquitted—not as an act of leniency, but as a matter of right. Since the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the appeals were allowed and the convictions were set aside.

Both the Rent Controller and the appellate court ruled in favor of the landlord, ordering eviction.

The tenant challenged these rulings before the Islamabad High Court, arguing (among other things) that no written, registered lease agreement existed and that he should not be evicted without one.

The High Court clarified several important legal points. First, an unregistered lease agreement cannot create legal rights in the property and cannot even be used as evidence of a landlord-tenant relationship. However, the court emphasized that this actually helps landlords, not tenants — if there's no written agreement, the landlord can seek eviction at any time. The court also ruled that failing to have a written agreement is not a valid defense against eviction.

Additionally, the court addressed rent deposits: if a landlord refuses to accept rent, the tenant must proactively apply to deposit it with the court to avoid being labeled a "defaulter." The tenant here had failed to do so.

The court also upheld that a landlord's father, acting under a valid power of attorney, could legally pursue the eviction case.

**What the case was about:**

He complained to the Wafaqi Mohtasib (Federal Ombudsman), alleging maladministration, but the Ombudsman dismissed his complaint. He then appealed to the President, who reversed the Ombudsman's decision and directed PIAC to accommodate him in the next training batch. title: Re-Investigation after commencement of Trial
explainer:
**What the case was about:**
Manzar Abbas, an accused in a criminal case (FIR No. 115/2020), challenged an official memo dated 20.05.2021 issued by the police (Respondent No. 8) directing re-investigation of his case. Abbas argued that since his trial had already begun—and the charge against him was formally framed on 07.05.2021—the police could no longer legally order a fresh investigation at that stage.

**What the court decided:**
The Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) agreed with the petitioner. It noted that the respondent police authority did not dispute that the trial had already commenced and the charge had been framed before the memo was issued. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent (2014 SCMR 1488), the Court held that while re-investigation or supplementary reports are generally permissible even after the initial police report, they cannot be ordered once the case has moved forward to trial and formal charges have been framed. The Court declared the police memo ordering re-investigation "illegal, without lawful authority, and having no legal effect," and allowed the petition.

**Why it matters:**
This ruling reinforces an important safeguard in criminal procedure: once a trial has begun and charges are framed, police cannot use re-investigation as a tool to interfere with or delay the judicial process. It protects the integrity of ongoing trials from executive/police overreach and clarifies the limits on police powers under the law once a case is before a court.

title: Lap of Mother is the best school for growing child
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over a young girl following her parents' divorce. Both the mother (petitioner) and father had remarried after separating. The father, a soldier, filed for custody, arguing the mother's second husband was related to the child within prohibited degrees and that she was being kept from visiting her father.

The Family Court initially sided with the mother, dismissing the father's custody application. However, an appellate court (Additional District Judge) reversed this, awarding custody to the father. The mother then challenged this reversal before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the mother, restoring the original Family Court decision. It reasoned that although the father was the natural guardian, practical circumstances mattered more for the child's welfare: the father's army service kept him constantly transferred and unavailable, and the child would effectively be raised by her elderly, ill grandmother or an unreliable stepmother. By contrast, the mother's second husband was closely related to the child and from the same family background, making that home more suitable.

The court emphasized the four-year-old girl had lived with her mother since birth and developed deep attachment to her, famously stating that "the lap of the mother is the best school for a growing child." It held that a mother's remarriage alone doesn't automatically disqualify her from custody when the child's actual welfare favors staying with her. This case reinforces that Pakistani courts prioritize the child's practical welfare over rigid legal presumptions in custody disputes.

title: Case of a double murder
explainer:
This case involves a violent altercation between two families in Sialkot, arising after one of the appellants, Muhammad Akmal, had divorced the complainant's daughter. Tensions escalated when the complainant's son was allegedly beaten by the appellants, leading the complainant's family to confront them the next day. The confrontation turned deadly — two men (Guftar Ahmad and Muhammad Aslam) were shot dead, and others were injured. The trial court convicted Muhammad Akmal and Muhammad Ajmal for double murder and attempted murder, sentencing them to death, while acquitting two co-accused.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony (from witnesses who were themselves injured) and medical evidence, finding both consistent with the prosecution's version. The appellants claimed self-defense, arguing the complainant's side attacked first out of anger over the divorce, but they failed to provide evidence supporting this claim, as required by law once such a plea is raised.

However, the court noted that both sides seemed to be hiding the true details of how the fight started, suggesting mutual concealment of facts. Because of this ambiguity about who provoked the incident, the court found "mitigating circumstances" and reduced the death sentences to life imprisonment, while upholding the convictions.

This case highlights how courts assess conflicting testimonies in violent family disputes and how the burden of proof works when self-defense is claimed, and how sentencing may be tempered when the full truth remains unclear.

title: Case of PAF inter college teachers
explainer:
This case involved teachers at Pakistan Air Force (PAF) Inter-Colleges who wanted the courts to declare them "civil servants," which would entitle them to the same benefits, protections, and facilities that government employees receive.

These PAF colleges were originally set up to educate the children of Air Force personnel, and were later opened to civilian students too. Their operations were governed by an Air Force Manual, which set rules for administration, academics, and staff employment. However, the Court found that each institution was actually self-financing—funded through tuition fees, not government or PAF grants—and was run by its own Managing Committee, which had full power to hire, promote, and fire staff. There was no provision for transferring employees between PAF institutions, and the Federal Government had no role in running them.

Because of this, the Supreme Court held that these colleges were essentially private institutions, even though some PAF officers sat on their governing boards. The teachers' jobs were created under the institutions' own internal rules, not under any law establishing government/civil posts. Therefore, the employment relationship was simply "master and servant," not government employment.

Since the teachers weren't civil servants, their case couldn't be heard by the Service Tribunal (which only handles civil servant disputes). The Supreme Court dismissed their appeals, meaning they were not entitled to civil servant status or benefits.

A government employee, Raja Muhammad Javaid, worked as Deputy Game Warden/Deputy Director Wildlife in Punjab since 1983 and had earned a postgraduate diploma in Wildlife Management. In 2003, the Punjab Government set promotion criteria for the higher post of Director Wildlife, requiring 12 years of service in one grade or 7 years in another. In 2007, the government amended these rules to add a new requirement: candidates must also hold an M.Sc. in Zoology or an equivalent qualification. The petitioner challenged this 2007 amendment, arguing it unfairly disadvantaged experienced officers like him who lacked this specific additional qualification, effectively blocking their promotion in favor of less experienced but more qualified candidates.

**What did the court decide?**

The Lahore High Court ruled in favor of the petitioner, striking down the 2007 amended rules. The court held that government rules affecting employees' rights must have proper legal backing and must be fair and consistent. Since the new qualification requirement disregarded years of dedicated experience and created insecurity among long-serving employees, it violated the constitutional principles of equality before law.

**Why does it matter?**

This case reinforces that government authorities cannot arbitrarily change service rules in ways that harm employees' legitimate expectations built on experience and existing rules. It highlights that fairness, consistency, and equal treatment must guide public sector decision-making, especially regarding promotions.

She wasn't unhappy about getting divorced; she only challenged losing her right to that unpaid dower.

**What the court decided:**

It explained that under Islamic law and Pakistani family law, a wife seeking khula must give up some benefit received from the marriage as consideration — usually by returning the dower already paid to her. But if she never actually received the dower (as in this case), she cannot simply keep her claim to it while also being granted a "cost-free" khula. Instead, giving up her *right* to claim that unpaid dower serves as the equivalent consideration. The court said the law's requirement to "restore" dower should be understood as including "relinquishing" her claim to it, since the two amount to the same sacrifice.

**Why it matters:**

This ruling clarifies that a wife cannot obtain khula while still keeping her dower claim — whether already paid or still pending. title: Fresh suit is barred in case of dismissal in default
explainer:
**What This Case Was About**

Abdul Haq claimed he had agreed to buy a house from Umar Din in 1975 for Rs. 6,000, paid Rs. 2,000 upfront, and took possession—with the remaining Rs. 4,000 to be paid upon registration of the sale deed. When Umar Din failed to complete the sale, Abdul Haq filed a lawsuit seeking a declaration that he owned the house. However, that first suit was dismissed for "default"—meaning it was dismissed because he failed to appear in court—and he never applied to have it reinstated.

After Umar Din died, Abdul Haq filed a second suit against Umar Din's legal heirs, again seeking a declaration of ownership, and this time also adding an alternative request for "specific performance" (a court order forcing completion of the sale). He argued this second suit was different because it had a different valuation and included a new alternative relief.

**What the Court Decided**

The court rejected this argument. It held that the "cause of action"—the core set of facts justifying the lawsuit—was identical in both suits: the same agreement, same payment, same possession, same refusal to complete the sale. Simply changing the valuation or adding an alternative prayer for relief didn't create a new cause of action. Under Order IX, Rule 9 of the Civil Procedure Code, once a suit is dismissed in default and not restored, a fresh suit on the same facts is legally barred.

title: Khulla is counted as a single talaq in Pakistan
explainer:
This case involved a husband and wife whose marriage had been dissolved by a Family Court through "khula" (a wife-initiated divorce, granted when she returns her dower to the husband). title: Judgment on a Loan taken from ZTBL
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Allah Ditta had taken a loan of Rs. 3,23,500 from Zarai Taraqiati Bank Limited (ZTBL) in 1993 to buy a tractor, to be repaid in 20 installments. He paid most installments, then the bank issued a relief/incentive notice allowing loanees to close their accounts early by paying the principal plus 20% (minus amounts already paid). Ditta paid the required amount under this scheme, but the bank refused to close his account, claiming the relief was only meant for defaulters who had missed at least two installments—not for someone like him who was short by just one installment. His lawsuit was dismissed by the Banking Court, leading to this appeal.

**What did the court decide?**

The Lahore High Court sided with Allah Ditta. It ruled that once the bank offered the incentive scheme and he accepted it by paying the required amount, he gained a legal right to have his account closed. The bank couldn't later say the offer excluded regular payers like him. The court set aside the earlier judgment and sent the case back to the Banking Court for a fresh decision.

**Why does it matter?**

The court criticized the unfairness of rewarding defaulters while penalizing honest, regular loan payers, calling it bad practice and contrary to equal treatment under Article 25 of Pakistan's Constitution. The judgment reinforces that banks must honor the terms of schemes they offer and cannot arbitrarily change conditions after customers rely on them.

title: Bank can not claim mark-up in decree
explainer:

The Bank of Khyber sued a borrower, Nazamuddin, to recover money owed under a financial facility (loan). To settle the dispute over exact amounts owed, both parties agreed to let a Chartered Accountant examine the accounts. The accountant's report showed that both the principal amount and mark-up (the Islamic banking equivalent of interest) were outstanding.

**The Borrower's Defense**

Nazamuddin didn't deny receiving the financial facility—he only argued weakly (and too late, during arguments rather than in his formal defense) that the facility was meant for his business, not him personally. Since he never properly denied taking the facility, the court disregarded this argument.

However, he raised a more serious objection: each time the facility was "rolled over" (renewed), the bank had charged mark-up on top of previous mark-up—essentially compounding it like interest.

**The Court's Decision**

The court agreed this was a legitimate concern. Charging mark-up upon mark-up would effectively turn an Islamic mark-up-based facility into a conventional interest-bearing loan, which is not legally permissible.

Faced with this, the Bank's own lawyer conceded and dropped the claim for mark-up altogether, asking the court to award only the principal amount identified by the accountant.

**Why It Matters**

This case reinforces that Islamic banking facilities must strictly avoid compounding mark-up like interest, protecting borrowers from banks disguising interest charges as mark-up when loans are

title: Limitation is six years where law is silent
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A man's late wife's family sued for the return of dowry articles (household items traditionally given to a bride) that were allegedly kept by the husband's family. The husband had died about 15 years before the case was filed, and the wife had reportedly been asked to leave her father-in-law's house six months after his death. Her petitioner (the father-in-law) argued the case was filed far too late — nearly 11 years after her right to claim the goods arose — and should be dismissed as time-barred under the Limitation Act, 1908, which allows six years to sue when no specific time limit is otherwise provided by law.

**What did the court decide?**

The Lahore High Court refused to interfere with the lower courts' decisions. On the limitation issue, the court noted that although courts have a duty to check limitation even if not raised by parties, the petitioner never raised this objection at the trial or first appeal stage. Since the wife claimed ongoing negotiations and community mediation (Panchayat) delayed the filing, this was a mixed question of fact and law that couldn't be raised for the first time in a writ petition after two rounds of litigation.

**Why does it matter?**

title: Judgement on Riba in Shariat Federal Court 1991 (First judgment)

This ruling was appealed, and in December 1999, the Supreme Court's Shariat Appellate Bench issued a detailed 600-page judgment upholding the prohibition on riba, confirming the same 28 laws were repugnant to Islamic law, and—importantly—laying out practical guidelines for transitioning Pakistan to an interest-free financial system (something the original 1991 ruling hadn't specified).

title: Appeal in Rent Cases

The Rent Controller refused, "struck off" (dismissed) the tenant's defence for non-payment, and ordered his eviction. title: PLJ 2015 Peshawar 277

Meanwhile, the trial court went ahead and issued the succession certificate to the widow, subject to her providing sizeable surety bonds—meaning she'd have to return her share if the civil court later ruled she was indeed divorced. The brother and sisters appealed this decision.

The Peshawar High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It relied on Section 373(3) of the Succession Act, 1925, which allows a judge to grant a certificate to whoever appears to have the "prima facie best title" even if there's a complicated rival claim, without waiting to resolve that dispute first. Since the marriage (Nikah) was proven and the alleged divorce wasn't proven in this summary proceeding, the widow was entitled to the certificate—with safeguards (the surety bonds) protecting the other side if the civil court later confirms the divorce.

title: Iftikhar Chodhary's Judgement on Preemption law from 2001
explainer:
This case is about a long-running property dispute involving Pakistan's pre-emption law (a legal right allowing certain people, like neighbors or co-owners, to buy property before it's sold to outsiders).

Sarfraz had won a pre-emption lawsuit in 1987, getting a decree to purchase land. The losing party (Muhammad Aslam Khan) appealed and got the price reduced, then filed a revision petition in the High Court—but later withdrew it. Years later, in 1992, he tried a different approach: filing an application under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, arguing the original decree was invalid because it was issued without proper jurisdiction, citing changes in pre-emption law (the old law had been declared un-Islamic and replaced).

The Supreme Court ruled against this challenge. It held that:
1. The application was filed too late (over five years later), while the law only allows about three years for such challenges.
2. Even when old pre-emption laws are replaced for being inconsistent with Islamic injunctions, ongoing court cases don't automatically become void—they continue under the law that was in force when they started.
3. The right to pre-emption is a substantive personal right that doesn't disappear just because the underlying law is later repealed.
4. People challenging even a "void" court order must act within a reasonable time, not years later.

The Court set aside the High Court's decision and dismissed the respondent's application, restoring Sarfraz's original decree. This case matters because it clarifies how legal rights and ongoing lawsuits are treated

title: Benefit of doubt goes to the accused
explainer:
This case involves an alleged kidnapping-for-ransom of a schoolboy, Muhammad Bilal, in Mianwali district in 2007. He was forcibly taken off his bicycle by men in a car. A ransom was reportedly paid, and he was recovered. Two men—Rafique Ahmed and Khalid Mehmood—were tried and convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court under laws on kidnapping for ransom, and both were sentenced to life imprisonment plus forfeiture of property. Both appealed, and the complainant also filed a petition challenging the sentence as too lenient.

The Lahore High Court examined the evidence separately for each appellant. For Rafique Ahmed, the court found the prosecution's case strong: consistent testimony, recovery of the car used in the abduction, and proof that ransom money was received. His appeal was dismissed, and his conviction upheld.

For Khalid Mehmood, however, the court found his defense—that he was merely a taxi driver uninvolved in the crime, and had stayed silent earlier only out of fear of being killed by co-accused—credible and consistent with what he had said throughout the case. Applying the principle that any reasonable doubt must favor the accused, the court set aside his conviction and acquitted him.

This case illustrates a fundamental rule of criminal justice: even in serious cases like kidnapping, each individual's guilt must be proven independently, and if genuine doubt exists, courts must lean toward acquittal rather than conviction.

title: Motive for benami transaction holds importance

The wife sued for possession, saying the property was genuinely hers. The trial court believed the husband and dismissed her suit, but the appellate court reversed this and ruled in her favor. The husband then challenged that reversal in the Lahore High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It explained that to prove a "benami" transaction (where property is held in someone else's name only for convenience, while another person is the real owner), the person claiming real ownership must show a credible motive for putting the property in someone else's name, along with proof of who paid for it, who possessed it, and who held the documents. Here, the husband had no legitimate reason to register the property in his wife's name, provided no proof he sent money for its purchase or construction, and never took steps to claim ownership himself. The court found the evidence pointed to the wife being the true owner.

This case matters because it clarifies the legal standards courts use to decide genuine ownership versus benami claims in property disputes, particularly relevant in family and

title: Talb-e-muwasibat holds great importance in the suit for pre-emption

This case involves a legal claim called "pre-emption," which under certain property laws in Pakistan allows a person with a superior claim (such as a co-owner or neighbor) to purchase land that has been sold to someone else, provided they follow specific legal formalities promptly.

To succeed in such a suit, the law requires the claimant to prove they immediately asserted their claim upon hearing of the sale—known as "Talb-e-Muwathibat"—and followed up formally, known as "Talb-e-Ishaad." In this case, although the plaint mentioned specific details, none of the witnesses testifying at trial confirmed the date, time, or place of the initial claim. Both the trial court and the appellate court ruled against the petitioner for this reason, and the Lahore High Court upheld those decisions.

title: Excellent Judgment on Rules of Business for Promotion
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Some senior civil servants (Basic Scale-21) went to the Supreme Court because they felt wronged when certain colleagues were promoted to Basic Scale-22 ahead of them. They argued the promotion process was unfair and didn't follow proper rules.

**What did the court find?**

The Rules of Business, 1973 require that promotion cases be sent to the Prime Minister through a proper, detailed summary prepared by the Establishment Secretary — clearly laying out relevant facts so an informed decision can be made. Instead, the government admitted that for about 60 years, this rule had simply been ignored in Grade 21-to-22 promotions. Files were sent to the Prime Minister without the required summary, and worse, the files of 267 eligible officers who were passed over weren't even placed before him. This meant the Prime Minister was only choosing from a partial pool, with no real comparison of merit or seniority among all eligible officers.

**What did the court decide?**

The Supreme Court ruled this was arbitrary and unlawful. It cancelled the promotion notifications, stripped the promoted officers of the benefits gained, and ordered that all Grade-21 officers be reconsidered afresh, properly and transparently.

**Why does it matter?**

The judgment reinforces that even though civil servants have no automatic right to promotion, they do have a right to fair, merit-based consideration, following proper legal procedure — not backroom arbitrary picks that undermine trust in the civil service.

title: Interpretation of Article 203-DD of Constitution
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over which criminal charge applied to a man accused of falsely alleging his ex-wife committed adultery.

**Background:** A woman (Mst. Durr-e-Shahwar Begum) filed a private complaint against a man (Haji Bakhtawar Said Muhammad), alleging he had accused her of adultery (zina) and bad character, claiming her three children were illegitimate. He reportedly made these accusations in written statements filed in her maintenance and dowry cases before the Family Court, and also before his elder brother and a village council (panchayat).

The trial court framed charges under Section 14 of the Offence of Qazf (Enforcement of Hadd) Ordinance, 1979 — a provision that applies when such accusations are made *during* a marriage. The trial court reasoned the allegations were made while the two were still married.

**The Court's Decision:** The Federal Shariat Court disagreed. It found that the marriage had already ended — the husband himself had admitted in his own court filings that he had divorced the complainant and executed a divorce deed. Since the accusations were made after the divorce, the parties were no longer husband and wife but simply "a man and a woman." This meant Section 14 didn't apply; instead, Sections 6 and 7 of the Ordinance (dealing with false accusations of adultery against non-spouses) were the correct provisions.

title: Can a respondent be deleted to not to be a party?
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over who must be included as a party (respondent) in a labour complaint concerning the registration of a workers' union.

The Army Welfare Sugar Mills Workers Union wanted the company's Management (General Manager) removed from a complaint filed by the Registrar of Trade Unions seeking cancellation of the union's registration. The Union argued that under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 2002, Management had no role in registration/cancellation matters and shouldn't be a party.

The Labour Court had already rejected this argument once (on an application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC), holding that since the cancellation complaint arose from information/representation provided by Management, the Management was rightly made a party. That decision was challenged in an earlier revision, which was disposed of without disturbing this finding. The Union then filed a fresh application—this time citing Order I Rule 10 CPC—seeking the same relief, which the Labour Court again rejected.

The Sindh High Court held that merely citing a different legal provision doesn't change the substance of the request, and courts look at the content of an application, not just the law cited. Since the issue had already been decided and upheld once before, filing another application for the same relief was unnecessary and would only delay proceedings, especially since evidence and cross-examination were already underway.

The Court dismissed the revision petition at the outset (in limine), emphasizing that repeated re-litigation of settled issues causes unjust delay in labour disputes.

title: Can the surety amount be reduced?
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A man named Mulazim Hussain had stood as a surety (guarantor) for an accused person named Faizan, who was facing a murder charge (Qatal-e-Amad) under Section 302/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code. When Faizan was granted bail, Hussain deposited savings certificates worth Rs. 100,000 as surety, promising to ensure Faizan appeared in court. However, after release, Faizan absconded and never returned to face trial.

The trial court forfeited the entire surety amount as a penalty for Hussain's failure to produce the accused. Hussain then approached the Sindh High Court, asking for the fine to be reduced, arguing he had acted purely out of goodwill (as Faizan was from his village) and received no financial benefit from standing surety.

**What did the court decide?**

The Sindh High Court rejected the request and upheld the full forfeiture of the surety amount. The court noted that once someone voluntarily agrees to be a surety, they take on a legal responsibility to ensure the accused's appearance in court — regardless of personal motives. Since Hussain failed to fulfill this obligation, he wasn't entitled to leniency.

**Why does it matter?**

The court relied on precedent from the Supreme Court, emphasizing that reducing surety amounts encourages accused persons to abscond and undermines the bail system. This case reinforces that sureties bear serious legal and financial responsibility, especially in serious criminal cases.

title: What is Inquest Report? What is the importance of Inquest Report?
explainer:
This case involved a young boy, Dilawar Hussain, who died at his home in Gujrat. His father (the tenant's landlord) accused the tenant, Saeed Ullah, of sodomizing and murdering the child, then hiding the body in a sack on a neighbor's rooftop. The trial court convicted Saeed Ullah of murder and sodomy, sentencing him to life imprisonment plus fines, while acquitting his wife and son (a minor) of related charges.

On appeal, the Federal Shariat Court acquitted Saeed Ullah, finding the prosecution's case full of doubts. Key witnesses weren't mentioned in the initial police report or "inquest report" (an early official record made when a death is reported, documenting cause of death and how it occurred). Their sudden appearance later in the trial looked suspicious. The complainant also changed his story over time, and no one could confirm the sack or body were reliably linked to the accused. The incident wasn't directly witnessed, and the one witness who claimed to see the accused carrying a sack was found unreliable ("a chance witness").

The court explained that inquest reports are crucial because they're prepared very early in an investigation, close to the time of death, and often reflect information given by the victim's own family—making inconsistencies with later testimony especially telling.

This case matters because it reinforces a key principle of criminal justice: convictions must rest on solid, consistent evidence proven beyond reasonable doubt—not suspicion, gaps in early reports, or later "improved" testimony.

title: International Lawyer Law Firm
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute among siblings, all descendants of a man named Anwar Khan. The property had earlier been divided by a revenue court, but some family members (respondents) challenged that division in civil court.

Following earlier court orders, the trial court appointed a local commissioner (a Tehsildar) to visit the property and carry out a fair partition. When the commissioner submitted his report, one party objected to it. However, the trial court simply confirmed the report without properly addressing these objections—it didn't record evidence from the objecting party, didn't take a formal statement from the commissioner, and didn't allow either side to cross-examine him.

An appellate court found this procedure unfair and sent the case back, ordering that a fresh local commissioner be appointed to redo the partition properly. The petitioner then challenged this appellate decision before the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court agreed with the appellate court's decision. It ruled that before confirming a commissioner's report over objections, a trial court must give the objecting party a real opportunity to present evidence and question the commissioner. Since this didn't happen, the appellate court was right to send the case back for a fresh partition exercise.

This case matters because it reinforces a basic fairness principle in property partition disputes: courts cannot rubber-stamp a commissioner's report when someone raises objections—they must allow proper scrutiny, including cross-examination, before finalizing decisions that affect people's property rights.

title: Amendment to the Pakistan Penal Code, Section 509
explainer:
This is not a court judgment but the text of a legislative amendment — the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2009, passed by Pakistan's Parliament.

**What it does:** The law amends Section 509 of the Pakistan Penal Code (1860), which dealt with "insulting the modesty" of women. Previously, this section used vague terms like "modesty" and "violate" that were open to broad interpretation and hard to enforce.

**Key changes:**
- It redefines the offense as "insulting modesty or causing sexual harassment," giving a much more detailed and specific description of what counts as harassment — including unwanted words, gestures, sexual advances, and intimidating behavior.
- For the first time, it explicitly extends protection to workplaces, not just public spaces like markets, streets, and public transport. Previously, Pakistani law had no specific provision covering workplace harassment.
- It increases the maximum punishment to three years' imprisonment, a fine of up to Rs. 500,000, or both.
- It also updates the Criminal Procedure Code so police and courts know how to handle such cases (e.g., arrest procedures, bailable/compoundable status).

**Why it matters:** According to the government's stated reasoning, harassment was preventing many Pakistani women from safely accessing education, healthcare, and employment. By closing the workplace gap and clarifying vague legal language, the amendment aimed to make public and professional spaces safer for women, encourage more women to join the workforce, and reduce poverty and gender-based bar

title: Further Inquiry is a strong ground for Bail
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Muhammad Tayyab was accused of cattle theft. He, along with four others, was allegedly involved in stealing a buffalo, ox, cow, and two calves worth Rs. 500,000 from a complainant in District Rahim Yar Khan. He was arrested and charged under Pakistan Penal Code sections dealing with theft (380) and dishonestly receiving stolen property (411). He applied to the Lahore High Court (Bahawalpur Bench) for post-arrest bail.

**What did the court decide?**

The court granted him bail. It found several weaknesses in the prosecution's case: the FIR was filed with an unexplained delay of one and a half months, there was no direct evidence linking Tayyab to the crime, and the reliability of the "recovery" of stolen animals allegedly found on him still needed to be tested during trial. The court also noted that simply having other criminal cases registered against him (nineteen, according to police) couldn't be used to deny bail, especially since prosecutors didn't show he'd actually been convicted in any of them.

**Why does it matter?**

The judgment reinforces an important principle in Pakistani criminal law: when a case appears to require "further inquiry" — meaning the evidence is unclear or disputed — bail should generally be granted, since bail is treated as a right rather than an exception. title: Administrator general's act amendment of 2012
explainer:
# Administrator General's (Amendment) Act, 2012 — Explained

**What is this?**

This is not a court judgment but a Punjab provincial law that amends an older statute called the Administrator General's Act, 1913. It became law in an unusual way: the Punjab Assembly passed it, the Governor sent it back for reconsideration, the Assembly passed it again, and when the Governor still did not sign it within ten days, it automatically became law under Article 116(3) of the Constitution.

**What does it do?**

The Administrator General's Act, 1913 deals with how the estates of deceased persons (their property, money, and assets) are managed by a government-appointed official called the "Administrator General," especially when no one has come forward to handle the deceased's estate through normal probate or inheritance proceedings.

This 2012 amendment updates the old law to fit Pakistan's post-1913 provincial structure. Key changes include:
- Confirming the law applies to the whole of Punjab (removing outdated references to "Divisions" or multiple provinces).
- Updating financial thresholds — for example, raising the value of small estates the Administrator General can handle without full probate from Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 100,000.
- Replacing outdated legal references, such as swapping the old "Companies Act, 1913" for the "Companies Ordinance, 1984."
- Simplifying language so the law consistently refers to "the Province" (Punjab) and "the High Court" (singular), rather than ambiguous references to multiple provinces or courts

title: Application for grant of exemption from attendance
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Tassawar Rasheed was facing criminal trial in two cases before a Magistrate in Chakwal for offences involving hurt and rioting (under various sections of the Pakistan Penal Code). During the trial, without seeking the court's permission, he left Pakistan for a job in Dubai. After leaving, he filed applications asking to be exempted from personally appearing in court under Section 540-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, citing his overseas employment. The trial court rejected his applications because he had already left the country without permission before even asking for exemption. His appeals (revisions) to the Additional Sessions Judge, Chakwal, were also dismissed. He then approached the Lahore High Court through a writ petition.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court dismissed his petitions. It held that an accused cannot simply leave the country and expect automatic exemption from attendance — he must wait for the court to formally grant such exemption before acting on it. Courts must assess each case individually and ensure they retain the ability to compel the accused's presence later if needed; granting exemption is not a mechanical formality.

**Why does it matter?**

The ruling reinforces that persons released on bail or facing trial cannot unilaterally decide to skip court proceedings by traveling abroad first and seeking permission afterward. This protects the courts' authority to control criminal proceedings and maintains public confidence in the justice system.

title: What is the time period for filing civil revision?
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A civil revision petition filed by the Government of Punjab was dismissed by the Lahore High Court on the ground that it was filed 35 days late. The High Court reasoned that: (1) the law specifically fixed 90 days for filing a revision, so the general provision allowing delay to be excused (Section 5, Limitation Act) didn't apply; and (2) the time spent obtaining certified copies of the judgment could not be excluded from that 90-day count because "revision" wasn't specifically mentioned in the relevant provision (Section 12(2)) of the Limitation Act. The Punjab Government appealed to the Supreme Court.

**What did the Supreme Court decide?**

The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court. It held that when the Limitation Act was originally written, no limitation period existed for revisions, so "revision" wasn't mentioned in Section 12(2)—not because lawmakers meant to exclude it, but because it was irrelevant then. When a 90-day limit for revisions was later added to the Civil Procedure Code in 1992, the Limitation Act was never updated to match. The Court ruled that time spent getting copies of the judgment should still be excluded when calculating the deadline. Once calculated properly, the Punjab Government's revision was actually filed on time. The appeal was accepted.

**Why does it matter?**

The judgment clarifies that even though a specific limitation period now exists for civil revisions, courts should still exclude time spent obtaining copies of judgments, and cour

title: PLJ 2012 Lahore 133 [Multan Bench Multan]
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A wife (the petitioner) had sued for dissolution of her marriage, along with claims for maintenance, dower, and dowry articles. When reconciliation attempts failed, the Family Court granted her a divorce on the basis of *Khula* (a wife's right to seek separation) on 31.1.2007. However, the court also ordered her to return the dower she had received at the time of marriage — Rs. 500 and five *tolas* of gold — as required by law when a divorce is granted through *Khula*. She challenged this repayment order in the High Court, arguing her husband never asked for the dower back and that she hadn't sought divorce purely on *Khula* grounds.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court dismissed her petition — not by ruling on the merits of the dower issue, but because she filed her constitutional petition four years after the original order. The court held that invoking the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction (Article 199) is an equitable remedy, and such long, unexplained delay ("laches") — which it called "contumacious lethargy, inaction, laxity and gross negligence" — barred her claim. Her excuses (bad legal advice, illness) were not accepted as sufficient justification.

**Why it matters:**

The case reinforces that even valid legal grievances can be lost if a person delays too long in seeking court intervention, and that courts expect diligence when invoking equitable, constitutional remedies.

explainer:
Dr. Muhammad Tahir-ul-Qadri, a Canadian-Pakistani citizen, filed a petition directly in the Supreme Court under Article 184(3) of the Constitution, challenging the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and members of the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP). He argued their appointments didn't follow the constitutional procedure (Articles 213 and 218), and asked the Court to declare these appointments void and order fresh, proper appointments before the upcoming general elections.

The Supreme Court dismissed the petition. It found that Qadri lacked "locus standi" (legal standing) to bring this case. Crucially, since he held dual Pakistani-Canadian citizenship and had sworn allegiance to Canada, the Court held he had given up certain political rights—including the right to be elected to parliament—even though he retained his Pakistani citizenship and other rights. More importantly, the Court noted he failed to identify any specific fundamental right that had been violated, which is required to invoke Article 184(3) jurisdiction. He also hadn't shown he approached the Court with genuine (bona fide) intentions rather than personal or other motives.

However, the Court did clarify that overseas Pakistanis, including dual nationals, retain the right to vote if properly registered on electoral rolls, and directed the ECP to ensure eligible overseas citizens are registered before elections.

title: Disobedient daughter is entitled for maintenance
explainer:
**What was the case about?**

A father (living in the UK) was challenged by his ex-wife and adult daughter for unpaid and ongoing maintenance. He had divorced the mother in 1987, remarried twice more, and allegedly stopped supporting the daughter. He argued he shouldn't have to pay because: (1) his daughter was educated, employed as a teacher, and could support herself; (2) she was "disobedient" because she refused an arranged marriage to his nephew; and (3) six years of back-maintenance was excessive.

**What did the court decide?**

The Lahore High Court rejected the father's arguments and upheld the maintenance orders against him. It held that under Islamic law, a father must maintain his daughter until she marries, regardless of her age, unless she has independent means to support herself. Importantly, the court ruled that even a supposedly "disobedient" daughter remains entitled to maintenance—there is no concept in Islamic law of disowning a child and cutting off their maintenance rights. The court also noted the father had failed to show he ever tried to maintain a relationship with his daughter, and that he was supporting children from his other marriages while neglecting her—amounting to discrimination.

**Why does it matter?**

This case reinforces that a father's duty to maintain his daughter is a continuing legal and religious obligation that doesn't disappear due to personal disagreements, disapproval of her choices, or claims she disobeyed him. It protects daughters from being cut off financially over family disputes.

The lower court (acting as a "Court of Protection") personally examined the grandmother and found her mentally sound. The judge found no evidence supporting the claim of mental disorder and strongly criticized the appellant's motives, calling the case a "crude and cruel effort" to seize the grandmother's rightful inheritance prematurely, rather than waiting to inherit it naturally after her death.

title: Wife cannot be compelled to live with husband whom she hates
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Kiran Sabah married Mushtaq Ahmed in 1993. She claimed that within a week of marriage, she discovered her husband was of bad character—that he brought strangers into the house, pressured her into an immoral lifestyle, and on one occasion beat her severely after she refused to have sexual relations with a stranger he brought home. She left the marital home and sought dissolution of marriage through "Khula" (a wife's Islamic right to seek divorce by giving up her dower), offering to forfeit her dower rights. Her husband denied these allegations and instead accused her family of taking dowry articles and cash when she left.

The Family Court and the Appellate Court (District Judge) both dismissed her case, ruling she had failed to prove her allegations.

**What did the High Court decide?**

The Sindh High Court accepted her petition, overturning the lower courts' decisions and granting her the divorce on the ground of Khula.

**Why does this matter?**

The Court held that a wife cannot be forced to remain married to a husband she has come to hate. If a court is convinced that a couple cannot live together as required within the bounds set by religion, they should be separated—even if the husband denies wrongdoing—so long as the wife is willing to give up her dower. The judgment reaffirms that Islamic law prioritizes divorce over forcing a woman into a marriage marked by hatred or immorality, reinforcing women's independent right to exit an unwanted marriage.

title: Even verbal Nikah is Nikah in Islam
explainer:
**Case Summary: Nabeel alias Raju Masih v. State (PLJ 2010 FSC 222)**

This case involved a young man convicted by a trial court for forgery, using a forged document, and Zina-bil-Jabr (rape) under Pakistan's Hudood laws. The background: a 16-year-old girl, Aneela Kausar, went missing after leaving her Quran classes and was allegedly taken away by the appellant and others. Her father filed a police complaint alleging abduction and rape. The appellant's defense was that he had actually married the girl through Nikah (Islamic marriage).

The Federal Shariat Court overturned the conviction. It held that even if a Nikah is not formally registered with the Union Council, this doesn't make the marriage invalid—non-registration is merely a separate offense, not proof the marriage never happened. The Court clarified that only Family Courts, not criminal courts, have authority to rule on whether a Nikah is valid or void.

Since there was no evidence the marriage had been declared void by a competent court, and evidence suggested the girl had gone with the appellant willingly (including letters and photographs showing them together), the Shariat Court found the rape and forgery charges unproven. The appellant consistently maintained he was married to her throughout the proceedings.

This case matters because it reinforces that a verbal Nikah, performed properly under Islamic tradition with witnesses and consent, is legally valid even without formal registration—and criminal courts cannot simply presume a marriage invalid to secure

**What was this case about?**

However, the Court ruled that since two contradictory guardianship orders could not both stand, the confusion had to be resolved by the Guardian Judge on merits, for the sake of the child's welfare. The petition was dismissed, and the matter was sent back for proper decision.

The police completed their investigation and filed a report ("challan") in court. However, the complainant was unhappy with how the police investigated the matter, so he separately filed his own "private complaint" covering the same incident. The trial court then summoned the accused in this private complaint case and began proceeding with that trial instead. As a result, the original police case (challan) became inactive, or "dormant," since the court's attention shifted to the complainant's private case.

The court ruled that going forward, questions about the accused's attendance would be handled under Section 91 of the Criminal Procedure Code within the private complaint proceedings instead. The court granted bail, requiring the accused to post a bond of Rs. 100,000 with one surety of equal value.
